en: Vādivāgīśvara:
O Mānamanoharā,
salutations to you who, by partaking of the nectar, have liberated those bound by the great elements.
That power, whose nature is consciousness, liberates even those who are established in the unmanifest (akula). // 1 //
This *Mānamanohara*, profound and intended to quell the pride of opposing disputants roaring in debate, is composed by Vādivāgīśvara, the son of the master Vāgīśvarācārya.
The Section on Accomplishment [Proof of Īśvara]:
1) The action under dispute is produced by a substratum of effort, because it is an action.
Whatever is an action is produced by that which is the substratum of effort, just like an action that is currently admitted;
likewise, the action under dispute is produced by that which is the substratum of effort;
therefore, it is produced by that which is the substratum of effort.
2) That which is the subject of dispute is corporeal and produced by effort,
because, while being distinct from atoms, it possesses corporeality.
3) Odor is produced by effort.
Because it possesses odor,
like a jar, and like the odor residing therein;
nor is there an equivalence of the reason (*prakaraṇasama*) by virtue of its not being produced by an embodied agent.
Nor is "being produced by that" a limiting adjunct (upādhi), because "not being an effect" is itself such an adjunct,
and because [the proposed adjunct] contains a redundant qualification.

By this, the claim that the ascertainment of pervasion occurs because [properties] such as being an action (*karmatva*) or being an effect (*kāryatva*) are seen even in isolation with respect to a sprout, its production, and so forth at the time of observing pervasion, is refuted; for the existence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) has not yet been determined.
As long as the limiting condition is not identified, [pervasion cannot be ascertained].
Therefore, even in the case of a single instance, one must state the causal necessity (*prayojakatva*) for the relation between these two;
for if a thing were to abandon the probandum (*sādhya*) despite having a relation not prompted by anything else, it would follow that it abandons its very nature (*svabhāva*),
since pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in a relation that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*).
4) Furthermore, when earth and water are held by one possessing effort, they do not fall despite having weight, like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand. 5) The knowledge of Īśvara is eternal.
Because, while being distinct from that which resides in both [the self and the body], it resides in God, like the greatness (mahattva) inherent in Him;
nor is there an equality of the reason with the subject (*prakaraṇasama*) by virtue of its being knowledge (*jñānatva*).

The condition (*upādhi*) is the existence of a cause; if that too were to be proven, there would be sublation (*bādha*). For there is sublation by scripture (*āgama*), as in: "For the seer, there is no loss of seeing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
Otherwise, one could also argue: "The color-form of a water atom is impermanent, because it is a color-form.
Nor can the presence of a cause be considered a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in that case either.
Because there is no sublation (bādhā) due to the proof of that [point] as well:
6) That which is the subject of dispute is produced by a substratum possessing eternal specific qualities (nityaviśeṣaguṇa), because it is an effect, like a water-dyad (āpyadvyaṇuka).
And that which is the substratum possessing eternal specific qualities—

That very one is Īśvara. 7) The proof of Īśvara against the Buddhist: The conceptual cognition under dispute is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) with respect to that which is distinct from it, because it possesses the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramātva*).
It is like non-conceptual valid cognition (*nirvikalpakapramā*).

Nor are there the fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) or the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because for devotees of Īśvara and others, there is the conceptualization of Him as the cause and so forth.
Various [phenomena] clearly arise, existing solely as latent impressions (vāsanā).
This is because you yourself have accepted [this] in [your work] *Tattvasaṃgraha* (verse 282), and it is all the more desired by me;
for in your own system, all cognitions possess the status of valid knowledge (*pramātva*) precisely by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*).
But for me, since there is no disagreement regarding the subject at hand:
8) this cognition is produced by a cognition that is distinct from the impermanent cause that produces it.
Because it is an effect,
like that which is commonly accepted;
nor is "being distinct from this" a limiting condition (upādhi) here.
For you, the qualification is useless;
for me, it is possible even in the case of eternal things. If the qualification "being an effect" is added, the aforementioned fault persists.
"God is the substratum of eternal knowledge; this is the definition of God.
Thus, God is established by such reasons as the fact of being an effect.
[Establishment of the Whole] 1) Conceptual cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) distinct from that which is non-conceptual,
because it possesses the nature of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramātva*).
Like non-conceptual valid cognition (*nirvikalpakapramā*): 2) This effect is produced by something distinct from the cognition that produces it, because it is an effect.
3) [The subject] is non-conceptual,
because it is produced by something distinct from the knowledge that produces the non-conceptual,
since it is an effect.
It is like other cognitions and like conceptual cognition;
nor is "being non-conceptual" a limiting condition (upādhi), because the qualification would be redundant.
Whatever manifests is cognition,
just as is commonly accepted;
the subject of dispute manifests, and thus there is no "parity of the argument" (*prakaraṇasama*) here.
Because a substratum established for both disputants is difficult to define;
by this, [arguments such as] "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) and so forth are refuted. [The subject: that which is under dispute is of the nature of cognition (*jñānātmaka*).
Because it is a real entity and because it exists, like that which is commonly accepted; thus,
the conceptualization of the gross is a valid cognition (*pramā*) with respect to an external object.
Because it possesses the nature of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramātva*), like the perception of color; thus, the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) is established.
Nor does the objection based on the dilemma of its mode of subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) and so forth arise [to refute this].
Because those very [arguments] are sublated by direct perception;
the sense faculty does not grasp substances,
because it is a sense faculty.

The argument "like taste," however, is not a valid proof because it is flawed by the fallacies of unestablished pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*), unestablished nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddhi*), and unestablished example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*).

This is because, as long as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is unknown, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be known, and furthermore, because the nature of a sense organ is a qualification of a substance.
Others, however, [argue that] smell has a non-smelly material cause.

They assert the proof of the composite (avayavin) on the grounds that it is an effect, like color; however, in that case, if the word "material cause" (upādāna) denotes the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), there is an absence of an example;
if it denotes merely something of the same genus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā).
If the two terms of the proposition denote that which is of an absolutely similar class, there is a contradiction between them.
The definition of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is "that which possesses parts and is characterized by tangibility.
[This leads to the proof of the atom (*paramāṇu*).]
1) The odor under dispute is produced by the cause of this [specific] odor, because it is an odor,
and because it is an effect, like that [other odor].
Nor is it a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the same manner as a physical mass (*piṇḍa*).

Because it would follow that the form and other qualities occurring at the same moment as that [cognition] would also possess such a nature. 2) A disputed effect is produced from this blue cause; [therefore, it is of the same nature].
Because it is an effect,
like the perceived blue;
nor is there an absence of supporting reasoning (anugrāhakatarka).
Even if one does not accept stable entities, the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) can be maintained;
for there is no basis for positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka).

If it is accepted that this [concomitance] is established through conceptual construction (kalpanā), then since the entity itself would be non-existent, the causal relationship rooted in it would also necessarily be non-existent, leading to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the entire universe is non-existent.

The argument that "because existence consists in causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is impossible for a capable [entity] to be delayed," and so forth, is to be refuted by the fact that [the delay] is conditioned by the presence or absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
[Objection: Let the auxiliary causes themselves be the cause [of the effect]. [Reply:
(If this is argued,) their utility would only apply if there were a fixed rule regarding their being the final [causes].

Because threads are utilized as delimiters even in cases such as the ultimate conjunction of threads, if they were not restrictive factors, there would be the undesirable consequence of cloth being produced elsewhere as well. Thus, the subject of dispute must be clarified: that which is stable and capable of producing an effect sequentially is [permanent], while its opposite is momentary.
3) The odors and other qualities under dispute cannot be the originators of earth,
because, while being distinct from conjunction, they are qualities of the elements, like disjunction.
Taste does not originate water; visible form does not originate fire;
and tangibility does not generate wind.
Sound is not the initiator of a substance, because it is a quality that qualifies an element (bhūta), or because it is a quality perceptible by a single external sense organ, like odor;
nor is there even a suspicion of this being due to an adventitious condition (aupādhika) in the case of "odor-ness."
Even in the absence of that [sound], the probandum is observed in cases such as gravity;
furthermore, for the final inference, being distinct from sound is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*),
nor is being distinct from taste a determining factor for the first [inference].
Because even conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other factors distinct from those [atoms] are observed to be initiators of water;
by this, the suspicion of an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) regarding the two middle [terms] is refuted.
Therefore, the existence of a material cause (*upādāna*) distinct from odor and the other qualities is established.
4) The effect under dispute has an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), because it is a positive effect (bhāvakārya), like a jar.
Nor is the qualification superfluous,
because the mere property of being an effect would be deviant with respect to destructions (dhvaṃsa) and the like.
5) Some [argue]: "The effect under dispute has an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), because it is an effect, or because it is large and corporeal, like a jar. [And:
"The effect under dispute is large..."
They assert that [atoms are eternal] because they are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

However, those [opponents], having understood through yogic perception, must qualify [the reason] as "for us and others" (*asmadādīnām*) in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding atoms.
And thus, the qualification is redundant (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Because there is no exclusion of the opponent [from the locus],
and because there is deviation with respect to the mind (*manas*);
therefore, the existence of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*) is established.
An atom is a corporeal substance that is not produced by other substances;
an atom is a corporeal eternal substance.
[The Section on Substances]
[The Examination of Earth] 1) That which is the subject of dispute has earth as its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), because, while being an effect, it possesses the nature of odor (gandhatva).
It would be like that which is currently accepted;

nor would there be the fallacy of being "conditioned by an extraneous factor" (sopādhikatva), because the property of being "great earth" (mahāpṛthivītva) does not pervade the probandum in the case of visible form and so forth.
Because "being an effect" (kāryatva), when qualified by "being distinct from that which is eternal and incorporeal," is possible even in the case of water and other such things;
because if it were qualified by "being earthen" (pārthivatva), the qualificand would be redundant;
and because if that which is free from adventitious conditions (nirupādhika) were to abandon the probandum (sādhya), it would follow that its very nature (svabhāva) is abandoned.
Therefore, there is a rule that an earth atom (pārthiva-paramāṇu) initiates only another earth [substance].
Being eternal and possessing odor, an earth atom is the definition of an earth atom.
2) The body of a deity is not non-womb-born (mayonija).
The reason "because it is a body" is inconclusive with respect to the bodies of locusts and the like. Furthermore, its possession of a specific configuration is unestablished for that [divine body],
because it is distinguished by various differences such as having three eyes, a thousand eyes, or four arms.
The series of bodies under dispute consists of bodies not born from a womb,
because it is a series of bodies,
like the series of bodies of a scorpion produced from cow dung.
Nor should one entertain favorable reasoning [to support the opponent's view], for otherwise it would follow that the meaning of the scripture itself becomes untenable, as the Śruti states:
"In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.121.1).
The body possessing fragrance is composed of earth;
3) the perception of fragrance is produced by a cause,
because it is an effect.
Like clarified butter that manifests the fragrance of saffron,
the nose is the sense organ possessing smell;
the earth is that which possesses smell.
Earth possesses color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, fluidity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*).
[The definition of water: The generality (*sāmānya*) of "water-ness" inheres in a body because it is a genus belonging to atoms, like existence (*sattā*).
The atoms under dispute are the indirect originators of the body, because they possess the nature of heavy atoms;
nor is "being an earth atom" a limiting condition (upādhi).
Even in the absence of that [specific unseen force], since the probandum is observed to follow [the cause] and there is no equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) in cases such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*),
others maintain that being drawn by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) is the operative factor even there.
And since that can be established by the previous inference, there is no fault whatsoever.
The body is composed of water (āpya), because it possesses the quality of cold touch.
The perception of taste is produced by an instrument (karaṇa), because it is an effect, just like the perception of smell.
The sense of taste is composed of water, because, like saliva, it manifests taste alone between the two qualities of form and taste;
the sense of taste possesses the quality of cold touch.
Water is a substance possessing viscidity (*sneha*).
Water possesses the qualities of color, taste, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum (*saṃskāra*).
[The definition of fire:]
1) The atoms under dispute are indirectly the originators of the body,
because they are material atoms,
like earth-atoms.

Nor can the argument "because it is not an earthly atom" be countered by the charge of *prakaraṇasama* (equivalence of the two sides) on the grounds that it is like the atom of the mind (*manas-paramāṇu*), for that would contradict scripture which states: "Having arisen from the oblations [made] to the divine source of fire, he goes upwards to the heavenly world with a golden body.
Nor is "being drawn by a specific unseen merit" (*viśiṣṭādṛṣṭākṛṣṭatva*) a valid *upādhi* (limiting condition), because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*).
The body is composed of fire (taijasa), because it possesses the quality of heat to the touch.
2) The perception of form is produced by an instrument, because it is an effect;
therefore, the eye is composed of fire.
Because it manifests only color (*rūpa*) among the two [color and taste], like light;
the sense-organ is hot and composed of fire (*taijasa*).
3) The atoms under dispute are not earthy (*pārthiva*), because...
Because it does not originate as ash when there is contact with extreme fire,
like a water atom;
that which is the subject of dispute is fiery.
Because it is a substance produced by atoms that possess a non-heat-produced color while being non-cold,
like fire as commonly recognized;
light possesses a hot touch.
Fire possesses color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and faculty (saṃskāra).
And thus is fire.
[The examination of air—
] 1) The atoms (belonging to air), which are the subject of dispute, are indirectly the originators of the body.
Because it possesses the nature of an atom that has tangibility,
like an acknowledged atom;
or, the body is composed of wind and is formless.

The body is the substratum of the contact with the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), given that it is corporeal and distinct from the tactile organ itself, and given its pervasiveness [in relation to the sense].
2) The perception of touch is produced by an instrument, because it is an effect, like the perception of color.
Furthermore, the tactile organ is composed of air (*vāyavīya*).
Between color (rūpa) and touch (sparśa), it is touch alone that has the nature of a manifesting substance,
like the fanning wind; therefore,
the sense organ is the tactile organ (sparśana), which possesses partless [non-material] form.
In the preceding [sections] and here as well, it should be understood that the object is a composite whole (*avayavin*) distinct from the body and the sense organs.
3) Air is not an object of direct perception for people like us, because it possesses the nature of air (*vāyutva*), like a subtle atom of air (*paramāṇuvāyu*).
Furthermore, atom-ness (*paramāṇutva*) is not the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
because the probandum is observed not to follow in the case of air-dyads (*vāyu-dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
Air is not an object of perception for people like us.
Because it is a substance devoid of form, like space.

Nor is "being a substance that lacks tangibility" a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), as it is absent in that very [instance] where the probandum exists.
Furthermore, the absence of manifested touch is not the determining factor when magnitude is present,
because it is absent in the case of light situated in water;
nor is that [light] perceptible either.
Because the error "the water is hot" would otherwise be untenable;
4) touch does not apprehend a substance devoid of color,
because it is an external sense organ, like the eye.

Nor is it correct to argue that air is not perceptible to people like us because, while not being a substratum for unmanifest color, it is a substratum for manifest touch, like a jar; for this argument fails due to the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of atoms.
Nor should it be qualified by the condition "provided that there is magnitude," because the presence of the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
And when this complex is analyzed, it does not exceed [the set of conditions consisting of] manifested color, manifested touch, and magnitude.
If that [reason] were to be established, it would result in a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Likewise, air is not perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves, because it is the substratum of number which is imperceptible to the senses of persons such as ourselves, like space (*nabhas*).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even this [air] is perceptible by the external sense-faculties,
because both are apprehended by the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Air is intangible and possesses touch.
Air possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and faculty.
[The examination of space: 1) The perception of sound, which is the subject of dispute, is produced by an instrument,
because it is an effect, like the perception of form.
And that sense organ is external because it illuminates external objects, like the eye.
Sound is dependent on something else,
because it is a quality, like color.
The substratum of sound is distinct from other [substances],

because it is the substratum of sound, unlike [other substances] such as visible form (rūpa). 2) Others, however, maintain that sound resides in a substance distinct from the eight [common] substances.
They argue that when an obstacle to its subsistence arises, [sound] must be distinct [from substance] because it possesses quality, like color.
This is incorrect, because the pervasion is not established;
for since distinction (vyatireka) is of the nature of a negation, its cognition is dependent upon the cognition of its counter-positive, which is the probandum.
Because inference would be redundant if that [absence] were already known.

Nor does this entail the abolition of all instances of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), for this fault does not apply in cases where the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

Because it is possible for there to be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) that possesses the greatness residing in space, the reason is not a purely negative one (*kevalavyatirekin*). Furthermore, if the probandum were formulated merely as "residing in something other than the eight substances," the reason would be over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*),
because universals such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) would also constitute similar instances, and the reason would be excluded from them.
3) That which is subject to misconception is not visible,
because it is a formless substance and because it is omnipresent.
Because it is always a substance devoid of touch, and because it is an eternal sense organ,
like the self and like the mind.
Space has the nature of form,
because, while possessing magnitude, it does not produce form, and because its magnitude is eternal.
Because it is a substance that is always devoid of tangibility, like wind and like the self;
[and] that which is disputed as being corporeal is conjoined with this [self], because it is corporeal, like that which is admitted [to be so].
The word "with this" refers to the subject under dispute.
4) Space possesses dimension, because it is conjoined [with other things], like a jar.
Nor is "possessing action" a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Because some things perish even though they have not performed an action,

nothing other than the loss of their fitness to serve as the substratum for that [action] remains; and since this is not due to being non-omnipresent, it is simply a particularity of dimension (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*).
Furthermore, a thing cannot be its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) with respect to itself, because you do not admit the existence of any probandum-form distinct from it;
moreover, non-pervasiveness (*asarvagatatva*) is possible even in the case of color and other such qualities.
If it were qualified by "substantiality" (*dravyatva*), the qualificand would be redundant.
If "possessing touch" (*sparśavattva*) were the determinant, it would follow that the mind (*manas*) lacks dimension,
because that [quality] is absent in the mind.
And we shall state that this [space] is atomic.
Regarding the argument that "space is not limited because it is inactive like a colored object," the limiting condition (upādhi) here is "not being a substance" (adravyatva).
5) Space is both conjoined and disjoined [with other things],
because it is a substance, like a jar.
Nor is "having parts" a limiting adjunct (upādhi) [for this inference].
Because it contains the reason stated by me,
and because the state of being produced exists when there is substantiality;
that very space, which is an all-pervading sense organ, is the auditory faculty (*śrotra*).
Furthermore, sound is not perceived everywhere in this manner; otherwise, it would follow that sound would be perceived whenever the bodies of the speaker and the listener are in proximity,
because that space delimited by the ear-cavity also exists there.
And the claim that "difference arises from the difference of limiting adjuncts" is a seed of error,
because there is no contradiction even if the self, the internal organ, and so forth were likewise [subject to such difference],
just as space is [distinguished] by sound.
[The definition of Space and Time: Like sound, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction, [Space and Time are established].
The conjunction under dispute is produced from substances that are devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa).
Because it is a conjunction,
like the conjunction of the two forms of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
that which is the subject of dispute is produced by two substances devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
Because it is an effect, just like that [other instance];
nor is "the state of being a conjunction of two internal organs" a limiting condition (upādhi),
because its qualification is redundant, for the same reason as before.
Nor is "being a quality of two internal organs" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
because since the [reason] is already established by the mere fact of being a quality of two, the qualification is redundant;
for that which is without a limiting adjunct [is the probandum].
If [the term] were abandoned, it would follow that its very nature is abandoned.

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension in including the plural number when the probandum is stated, because the example is unestablished; for since the *Bhūṣaṇa* does not accept number, the possibility of [the property] residing in the mind is far removed.
In the proof that "the mind is not conjoined with the mind because it is an eternal substance," the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is unestablished.
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya states that [the mind] does not initiate a substance because it lacks tangibility, by way of accepting conjunction.
Otherwise, he would have stated the absence of conjunction with its own kind as the reason alone.
This is because conjunction is a cause [of cognition].
And thus Vyomaśiva says: "By means of another's mind, one connects the mind residing in the subtle body with the self through a specific restriction.
Nor is there any lack of certainty [in this argument].
Because the conjunction with the unborn [soul] is unestablished;
nor is it correct to argue that the subject of dispute is not produced from two substances devoid of specific qualities,
because it is distinct from the conjunction with the internal organ, like space.
Regarding the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being non-produced:
"And those two are designated as space and time" means that space and time are endowed with number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.
"Because it is omnipresent"—this is to be proven as before.
[The investigation of the self: The "I-notion" under dispute is a valid cognition with respect to something other than the "I-notion," because it is a valid cognition.
Just as in the case of that which is currently perceived—
[namely, that the self alone is the substratum of cognition]—
when considering what its object is, one must specify "where it is itself inherent" in order to avoid the over-extension [of the definition] to the bodies and selves of others.
Since it has been established that it must be stated that this [soul] alone is its object—
[it follows that] the body is not inherent in it (tatsamavāyi), because it is an effect, like a jar.
Moreover, bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),

because even in the absence of that [bodilessness] in a dead body, one observes the concomitance (*anugama*) between the probandum and the probans. Nor is being a living body (*ajīvaccharīratva*) a limiting adjunct.
Because that [consciousness] is absent even in a living body during deep sleep, there is no fault, since the subject of the inference (*pakṣa*) is a body characterized by a particular state;
likewise, it should be stated: "because it is a body, like a dead body."
The vital breath under dispute is not the substratum of cognition,
because it is an effect, because it is air, and because it is breath— just like the vital breath in the state of deep sleep.
That which is the subject of dispute is produced from a substratum of consciousness, because it is an effect, like bodily movement.
Nor is there sublation by non-perception of the capable, since a substratum of consciousness, like a substratum of effort, can also exist as something capable [of being perceived].
If it is argued that consciousness, like whiteness and so forth, is not established through the perception of another,
because that which is qualified by it is beyond the senses, and because the mind lacks the capacity to apprehend another's consciousness;
whereas the body, however, is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible— then [we reply]:

And what follows from this? If it is argued that because consciousness alone is the substratum of awakening, in its absence there would also be an absence of the substratum of awakening—that is not so, because such a restriction is unestablished.
If it is argued that this is not the case because [consciousness] is all-pervasive (vyāpta), [we reply: no.
In that case, sublation by inference must be stated;
however, in that regard, the determination of the locus is difficult to establish:
"That which is the subject of dispute does not arise from a substratum of cognition."
The argument that [sound] is not produced by the body because it is like space has already been refuted.

Even if one maintains the "limiting condition" (upādhi) of being produced by the body, one must admit that it is preceded by a substratum of consciousness in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as the movements of a dead body.
Furthermore, the qualification "provided it is distinct from that [consciousness]" must be added.
In that case as well, since the qualification "while awake" must be introduced to avoid deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the bodily movements and so forth of one who is in deep sleep,

here too the term "acting" (kurvataḥ) must be stated to exclude the spontaneous, accidental actions of one who is indifferent. Otherwise, it would merely state an excessive effort on one's own part, and the uselessness of the qualification has already been mentioned previously.
This objection certainly applies on the grounds that a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is a property inseparably connected with the nature of the property to be proven;
otherwise, it would not apply even to other forms of inference.
For when a relation that is free from limiting conditions constitutes pervasion (*vyāpti*), once that limiting condition is destroyed, [the pervasion fails].

I have already stated that when a relationship has been observed in one instance, the observation of the mere reason (hetu) elsewhere does not constitute a fault; this is sufficient [for the refutation of Prabhākara’s view].
Others, however, assert that the self is established as the grasper in all cognitions of objects;
that is incorrect, because it would follow that the self is visible,
since its very nature consists in being manifested in the cognition produced by that [visual organ].
And if even a formless substance were visible to the eye,
then it would follow that space (*nabhas*) would likewise be so; furthermore,
the self does not manifest in visual cognition because it is a formless substance, like space.

If it is argued that "the cognition under dispute has the manifestation of a self, because it is a cognition, like the well-established 'I'-cognition," this is not so, because the argument is subject to the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadeśa* (proving what is already refuted by perception).

For instance: there is indeed, among the Buddhists and their disciples, a turning away from sense objects due to the impression of selflessness (*anātma-vāsanā*), and an engagement [with them] due to that same impression of selflessness.
And it is not the case that these are necessarily rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between the rope and the snake, or due to delusion, or due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver, or due to delusion, there would follow the consequence that these two [the rope-snake and the mother-of-pearl-silver] never arise;
yet they are neither non-ceased nor are they active.
Furthermore, neither cessation nor activity preceded by ignorance is possible for one who is established in their true nature;
nor is such [ignorance] tenable for them once there is knowledge of the Self.
Thus, it is determined that in the state prior to practice, the determination "Who am I? is untenable.
Because if it were non-determination, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "relation" (*sambandha*) when that [object] appears?
Is it the state of being an object (*karmatva*), or something distinct from that?
In the first case, there is an abandonment of a tenet (*apasiddhānta*); in the second, the example is unestablished (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*).
Furthermore, the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is not distinct from the first [case].
But if there exists the state of being grasped by a grasper, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Therefore, a separate, pervasive relation alone is not established.

Furthermore, when the visual cognition of objects such as atoms and forms during the state of dissociation for yogins is made the subject (*pakṣa*), your [argument] suffers from the fallacy of the locus being unestablished in part (*āśrayaikadeśāsiddha*).

Otherwise, our argument would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Nor does it follow that self-cognition must occur even during the state of deep sleep simply because the causal complex for mental perception is always present; for you yourself must admit that in cases such as the failure to grasp the distinction between "I" and the body, the entire group of causal factors distinct from the external senses is required for the arising of the cognition "I. It is by the power of those very factors that everything is accounted for.
Or, due to a deficiency in such karma,
there is no manifestation of the self in all cognitions [of those who possess omniscience].
[The refutation of the self being of the nature of knowledge:
Furthermore, that [self] is the substratum of knowledge, but it is not itself of the nature of consciousness;
for "there is no loss of the vision of the seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
Thus, because the relationship between the seer and the vision is perceived in the Śruti,
and what is perceived in the sacred tradition cannot be erroneous due to its lack of distinction [from other valid knowledge],
nor is there an absence of denotative power regarding established facts (siddhārtha).
Because it would result in a contradiction with one's own tenets; nor is it the case that [the scripture] is not intended for that [purpose],
since, as that [purpose] is not established by any other means, the scripture is intended for that specific qualified [meaning].
Nor is this a case of metaphorical usage, as in the expression "Rāhu’s head," because there is no subverting evidence against the primary sense;
nor does the scriptural teaching of non-duality (advaita) constitute such subverting evidence.

On the contrary, in the opposite case, it actually possesses the capacity to grasp difference. Nor should it be said that it lacks such capacity there, for as long as the capacity exists, there is no contradiction.
Nor is there an impossibility of apprehension in the absence of a relation, because that is not a defect; nor is there an over-extension [of the principle],
because non-apprehension serves as the restrictive factor.
Because [the cognition] is restricted when the presence of the causal complex other than that which is occasioned by the counter-positive and the knowledge of the counter-positive both exist;
or alternatively, because the connection with the specific instrument itself is the restrictor.
For instance, the cognition produced by an eye in contact with a jar apprehends only the jar, and not any other object.
Because it is unconnected [to reality].
Furthermore, this conventional consensus exists, as evidenced by the statement: "It is precisely for this reason that we engage in worldly discourse."
And if that [difference] were to lack a cause, it would be eternal;
however, difference is not thus imperceptible,
because existence belongs only to that which is the object of a correct, immediate experience.
And since the permanence of these three is established,
there is no departure from our own tenet (apasiddhānta), for we too establish the permanence of cognition.
Nor does an infinite regress of differences constitute a refutation,
because there is no basis for it when further differences are entailed;
for we observe in worldly convention that "the difference and the thing differentiated are distinct."

Nor can the inference of one particularity be established by the force of another particularity, because there is no fault in its arising provided that the distinction of the example remains unimpaired;
this is like someone who has gone to beg for oil-cakes being forced to accept a gift of a *khārikā* measure of oil instead of vegetables and the like.

If the distinction of the example is undermined, then inference does not arise at all, because it is sublated by that very [example] due to its superior force as that upon which the inference depends; furthermore,
this constitutes a "pseudo-reason" (jāti) because it contradicts its own nature.
By this, invisibility and other such qualities are refuted;
nor is difference indeterminable, because there is a lack of evidence for that.

If it is argued that the means of valid cognition is the impossibility of appearance and sublation occurring otherwise [than through the reality of the object], we reply: since there is no contradiction when these can be accounted for otherwise, and because it is impossible for what is non-existent to appear; [therefore, this is not a valid proof].
If it is argued that because sublation is impossible for that which exists, both [existence and sublation] are observed here,
we say no; for if the word "non-existent" (asat) conveys a meaning in the first case, there is a contradiction with the statement "because of the impossibility of appearing."
Otherwise, there would be meaninglessness, because there is a rule that the meanings of words employed must function in combination.
As for the second [alternative], what is the meaning of "of that which exists"?
Does it refer to that which is endowed with existence, or rather to that which is uncontradicted,
or to that which has the nature of Brahman?
Where has pervasion been observed in the first case— that of that which is endowed with existence— by way of its being uncontradicted?
For the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is subject to contradiction, and Brahman, being devoid of attributes, lacks [empirical] existence.
In the second case, there is non-distinction from the probandum;
in the third, there is the proving of what is already established.
Therefore, even indeterminability [of the object] is not tenable.
[Refutation of the Theory of Non-Segmented Meaning (Akhaṇḍārthatva):
By this, that which the Ekadaṇḍins say is refuted— namely, that words such as "Satya" (Truth) refer to an indivisible reality because they constitute a definition-statement (lakṣaṇavākya).
This too is refuted, as in the cases of "the earth possesses fragrance" or "a pot is a jar."
The meaning is that [the word "Brahman"] has an unbroken, supreme, eternal sense that is neither deficient nor redundant; for this is what "yataḥ" (from which) signifies.

Furthermore, under the view that [Brahman] possesses parts, the simultaneous use of words such as "satya" (truth), "jñāna" (knowledge), and "ānanda" (bliss) would not be logical, because they would be synonyms.
If they were not synonymous, non-duality would be lost.
Nor is it tenable to claim that even with two words, as in "the sun is the supreme light," only a single object is conveyed,
for the supporting example is unestablished.
This is because the word "superior" (prakṛṣṭa) functions by depending on a cause such as mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva),
whereas the word "illumination" (prakāśa) functions by virtue of its own nature as illumination;
otherwise, the same objection would apply to that case as well.
Furthermore, in the world, the words "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) and "light" (*prakāśa*) are used separately— as in "an excellent man" (*prakṛṣṭaḥ pumān*) and "a lamp is light" (*pradīpaḥ prakāśaḥ*).
However, when both are employed together for a single object, such as the sun (*mayūkhamālī*), they convey a specific meaning.

But this is not the case for the words "knowledge" (jñāna) and "bliss" (ānanda), because even worldly knowledge and bliss possess the nature of Brahman. If they were derived as distinct entities, the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) would be shattered.

Therefore, the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is employed in the sense of the mere absence of suffering, because there is a sublation of its primary meaning; for it is stated in scripture: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
Nor does this have the purpose of negating worldly happiness, for both types of happiness are absent; moreover,
it is admitted that even in the world there is a perception of supreme bliss to some degree.
Nor is it for the purpose of negating delimited pleasure here;
for even there, it is the delimitation itself that is negated, not pleasure.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the restriction of a general term.
Nor is the scriptural passage concerning Ānanda a valid means of knowledge, because its meaning is figurative;
nor is there a contradiction.
Because bliss (*ānanda*) would necessarily be impermanent due to its non-perception at all times, its status as liberation (*mokṣa*) would be contradicted;

furthermore, it is logically consistent to understand it as referring to a specific excellence of pleasure capable of being enjoyed for a long duration, attained through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of yoga.

As for the scriptural texts concerning its "endlessness" (*anantatva*) and so forth, they should be explained in terms of a very long duration relative to other forms of happiness that are merely comparative.
It is like the expression "the gods are immortal" (*amṛtā devāḥ*).
Nor is there any impossibility of engagement [in activity], for such engagement would be even more impossible if [the self] were eternal.
For no one exerts effort here for the sake of producing what is already established.

If it is argued that [effort is made] for the purpose of removing delimitation (*avaccheda*), then, for one who distinguishes between what is attained and what is not attained, the very removal of delimitation is the intended goal of the action here.
Because even that which exists in another is not a determining factor;
furthermore, in the doctrine of a single eternal pleasure, the appropriation of causes is not tenable—
what then can be said regarding its specific variations?
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to attribute both excellence and non-excellence to a single entity,
as that would contradict its oneness.
It must be stated that the specific cause is employed for the purpose of excluding [other] limitations.

Furthermore, regarding the objection stated— that since the experience of the absence of suffering as pleasure is unsurpassed, that [pleasure] is untenable— that fault applies equally here. Therefore, one must accept that pleasure is produced by the investigation of means for achieving pleasure distinct from the mere absence of suffering, and that it is impermanent and manifold.
Furthermore, for such a being, the possibility of discourse regarding liberation does not exist;
moreover, the word *jñāna* denotes a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "that in which it is known.
Furthermore, infinity (*ānantya*) is simply the absence of both limits.
For it is precisely there that worldly convention arises;
and the word "one" (eka) is intended to exclude duality, or rather, it expresses the numerical category of oneness.
Because linguistic usage occurs only in that regard within the world, and because the Veda conveys meaning through powers understood from worldly usage;
therefore, it is established that the Self is the substratum of cognition.
[The plurality of the self—
] That which is the subject of dispute is connected with me because it possesses form,
like my own body; thus, its eternity, beginninglessness, and omnipresence are established.

And it possesses multiplicity, because otherwise its systematic arrangement would be inexplicable; furthermore, since the theory of the indivisibility of the self has been refuted, there is no disagreement regarding the distinction between individual souls.
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree;
one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
Thus says the Śruti. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)
The meaning of this is as follows: "Two birds" refers to two selves who are "joined together," meaning existing together as "companions" because they perform a single common purpose;
they have both "embraced the same tree," that is, the single body.
Between those two selves, "one"—the enjoyer—"eats the sweet fig," meaning he experiences a particular kind of pleasure.

"The other, not eating" means the non-enjoyer, the Lord, "shines forth intensely on all sides"; thus, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is clearly established. "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—the one unborn male, rejoicing, lies beside her; another unborn male leaves her after she has been enjoyed."
As in the case of Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5,
that which is perceived through scripture cannot be otherwise.
How then [is one to understand] the statement, "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)?
Thus [it is said], and also from the indicative mark: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.10).
This is because the designation [of "self"] occurs through the presence of those [aggregates] when diversity is perceived.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that a figurative usage (upacāra) proceeds only when there is a purpose and a basis,
for in this case no such purpose exists.
Because the rule is not established;
for that [rule] is absent in cases such as *yava* and *varāha*, where words are used figuratively toward things whose primary meanings are unknown,
and also in the case of the word *go* when used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) to indicate mere existence (*sattā*).
For example, "the Vāhīka is an ox.
As the authors of the Vārttika have said: "[Metaphorical expressions] depend upon the distinctions of many classes, qualities, substances, and actions."
The conditions that arise suddenly, consisting of both the literal and the indicative.
The world does not seek to determine [the truth] due to a lack of causes;
however, those who know the Vedic texts analyze it for the sake of establishing strength, weakness, and so forth.
For reflection is indeed directed toward figurative cognition such as our own;
what is this insistence regarding figurative usages that have entered common practice through the linguistic behavior of elders?
As for the expression "oil in mustard seeds," one should not suspect that it is a metaphorical usage because there is no contradiction regarding the primary sense;
for the distinction [between the two] is perceived through both direct perception and scripture.

The self is manifold due to its distinction as the substratum of various subordinate universals distinct from the universal "substance-ness," because it is the locus of specific qualities that are not audible,
like earth and the other elements.

In that case, corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is not the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because even in the absence of that [corporeality] in color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, one observes the concomitance with the probandum (*sādhyānugama*). Makaranda, however, [states]: "The bodies under dispute..."
They possess a single self,
because they are bodies,
just like my own body.
Its permanence [is established].
Its specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) are to be proven by its being a substance.
Its qualities are: cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, mental impression (bhāvanā), number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
The self is the substratum of effort.
[Regarding the definition of the mind: That which is the subject of dispute is the object of sensory cognition produced by the senses.
Because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a jar.
The subject of dispute is the substratum of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) for which conjunction with a corporeal substance (*mūrta-saṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*),
because, while being eternal, it possesses an impermanent specific quality.
It is like an earth-atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*).
Nor is "reality" (*tattva*) a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
because in your view, even a jar is a substratum for specific qualities produced by contact with fire.
Nor is "earthiness" (pārthivatva) a limiting adjunct (upādhi), because even a jar, according to your own view, is a substratum for specific qualities produced by contact with fire.
Nor is "earthiness" a limiting adjunct.
Because there is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of an unbaked or destroyed jar; nor is our first [proposed] limiting condition (upādhi) valid,
because we observe the presence of the probandum even in the absence of that [condition] in the ether (nabhas).
Some maintain that the mind is an atom, because it is eternal while being the substratum of an inherent cause for the specific qualities of another [substance], just like a fiery atom.
That is not so, because "being eternal" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) when [the probandum] is "possessing touch.
When proving merely "atomicity," "not being large while possessing touch" is the limiting condition. And when proving merely "corporeality," the inclusion of the word "eternal" is redundant.
In the view of the author of the *Kāśikā*, if that which is distinct from those [two] were the cause, then "possessing touch" (*sparśavattva*) would be the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

In the position that darkness is a substance, since "possessing touch" pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in darkness itself, "being a substance inherent in a substance" (*dravyasamavāyidravyatva*) is the limiting condition.
By this, the argument that "the mind is corporeal because it possesses conjunction with an omnipresent entity, like a jar" is also refuted.
Because it possesses the aforementioned qualification:
pleasure and the like have conjunction with a corporeal substance as their non-inherent cause,
because, while being non-eternal, they are eternal specific qualities.
The argument "like the form of an earth atom" is not a valid proof because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of sound produced from disjunction (*vibhāga-ja-śabda*).
If the qualification "provided it is not sound" (*aśabdatve sati*) is added, it is redundant for the opponent.
Furthermore, the argument "the mind is corporeal (*mūrta*) because it is a sense organ other than the auditory organ" is also refuted.
Regarding the previously mentioned condition (*upādhi*):
if [the subject] were non-pervasive (*avibhu*), then "possessing touch" (*sparśavattva*) would be a condition that pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans.

By this, the argument of Śrīvallabha—that "possessing touch" is not a condition for proving "non-magnitude" (*amahattva*) by means of the reason "being a pervasive eternal substance" because it does not pervade the probandum—is refuted.
And the mind is not all-pervading,
because (1) it is a substance that is always devoid of contact,
and (2) it is a substance that is always devoid of specific qualities.
3. Because it is an indivisible sense organ;
4. because it is an eternal substance that does not originate other substances; 5. because it is an eternal sense organ.
6. Because it is a sense organ that serves as the substratum for the conjunction which is the inherent cause of consciousness;
7. because it is a substance that is always devoid of touch; 8. because it is a sense organ that perceives eternal qualities.
Because, while being unreal, it has the nature of truth,
like time,
like the self.
Regarding the refutation by means of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) that [the mind] is like space, it must be asked: how can one's own position be established?

For if the all-pervasiveness of the mind is accepted, it is impossible to prove anything other than space and time; thus, the argument is necessarily beset by either sublation of the evidence apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*) or the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). This is even more evident in our *Nyāyalakṣmīvilāsa*, where the proponent of darkness as a substance (*tamodravyatvavādin*) faces the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in that very same context.
And because the term "always" (sarvadā) would be redundant;
by this, the second and third [alternatives] are refuted,
and the seventh is also rendered useless.

In the ninth [case] as well, the term "formless" (arūpi) is redundant for the opponent, because darkness is non-existence (abhāva). What more need be said? The limiting condition (upādhi) is: being a substance that belongs to the same genus as a substance perceptible by the senses, under a sub-genus of the genus "substance-ness."
1. The mind is an atom, being devoid of touch; or 2. it is corporeal, being the substratum of the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of cognition;
or 3. it is the sense-organ that apprehends pleasure.

4. either the subtle sense organ (*aṇvindriya*), or 5. the insentient mind (*manas*) which is the substratum of the conjunction that produces knowledge, or 6. the sense organ which is the substratum of the non-inherent conjunction [of knowledge].
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and faculty (saṃskāra).
Their establishment follows from [the atom's] corporeality and substantiality.
Substance is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
2. A substance possessing qualities.
[10. Examination of the claim that darkness is merely the absence of light:
1) Darkness is indeed a distinct substance.
If it is argued that even this must be investigated, we say no, because it is not established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the cognition "darkness is blue" is the valid means of cognition, [we reply: no.
Because the cognition of "blue" is not established.
And it has been stated by Śālikanātha as well: "This is merely an illusion of cognition among the dull-witted regarding that which is actually uncognized" (*Prakaraṇapañcikā* 321).
If that is so, how then is there the employment of words?

If it is argued that the worldly usage "the non-black is blue" occurs through metaphorical application (upacāra) because of the absence of white, and that this is so because there is no sublation (bādhaka) regarding the primary sense;
Because it is not established that the eye, independent of light, can produce the cognition of form;
for it is impossible that an effect should arise in the absence of its cause. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even a blue jar [in total darkness].
If it is asked, "How then does the delusion of a black snake arise in the shadow?", [the answer is: "Due to a defect (*doṣa*).
A defect is that which superimposes a previously perceived black snake.
If it is asked, "What is the similarity (*sādṛśya*) here? [the answer follows].
It is the state of having the appearance of white.
Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
because it is not established that mere similarity alone constitutes the causal complex for erroneous cognition.
For even factors such as the non-perception of specific features, which operate in conjunction with the absence of light, as well as qualities like *dharma* and so forth,

and defects such as the contact of the sense organ with curved or elongated parts, are utilized [in the production of error]. Alternatively, some maintain that it is purely mental, as in the case of dreams, delusions, and the like.

And there is no such over-extension [of the principle], because even in the absence of visual light, it is admitted that the specific recollection of elephants, horses, and so forth serves as the cause for that [recognition]; thus, there is no over-extension.
By this, the perception of number, action, and so forth is also refuted.
Because there is disagreement on that very point, because the employment of words can be justified even through metaphorical usage, and because worldly convention is inherently consistent.

3) Furthermore, the proponents of the "partial" view (*ekadeśin*), while accepting the cognition of blue, declare it to be erroneous. As they say in the section on error: "The darkness of night is like a mass of collyrium. We observe that in this case, because the appearance is not subject to sublation (*bādhā*), it is difficult to establish a sublater; for since the object has been removed by this [cognition], the sublater itself fails to arise.
4) And it is the means for establishing cognition even without a word.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the meaning of the word *tamas* (darkness)?", [the answer is:
it is the absence of contact with light, as admitted by both disputants.

If it is argued that even when a particular light exists, there is the possibility of the absence of other lights, and thus the application [of the term "darkness"] would follow as a logical consequence; to that we reply:
in that case, does the application of the term for the absence of light exist or not? If it does exist, then let the application of the word "darkness" also exist—what loss is there for us?
This is because they are synonymous terms.

Alternatively, just as in the case of a flame, although its destruction occurs midway due to its extremely rapid perishability, there is no conventional usage of "destruction" because it is obscured by the arising of a similar flame; likewise, when light is present, although there is an absence of other light, there is no conventional usage of that absence because it is obscured.
But worldly consensus is said to be erroneous.

This is equally [inapplicable] to you who possess a mind hardened by logic; for your stated refutation—that "the sense organ which perceives colored objects, when not assisted by light, is a substance-perceiving organ because it is a sense organ that perceives substances, like the skin"—is rendered inconclusive by the olfactory organ (which perceives time), and the qualifying attribute is redundant.

In the proof that "the eye grasps a substance independently of light because it is a sense faculty," the opponent intends to point out the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by means of the sense of smell—both in terms of its being a prover and its being a probandum.

For you [the proponent] do not hold that such a thing is exclusively characterized as darkness; rather, this is because time (*kāla*) and other factors are also graspable by sense faculties independent of light.
5) Since the nature of light is admitted by both disputants, there is no disagreement regarding its being denotable by the word "darkness," nor is any further argument required here.
The light under dispute is denotable by the word "darkness," because it is an absence of light distinct from mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
If it does not exist in this way, then it does not exist even in that way,
just as in the world.

Others, however, maintain that darkness is the absence of light, because it is perceived even when there is no inferential mark (liṅga) or other such means, provided the eye is present and independent of light— just like the absence of light which is commonly admitted.
In this regard, what are the "similar" (pakṣa) and "dissimilar" (sapakṣa) cases?
It must be considered whether they are different or non-different;
furthermore, because [the subject] is perceivable by the minds of yogins, it is impossible to establish a definitive determination, and thus the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha).
Therefore, the sequence of the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the term "darkness" denotes the absence of light,
because it denotes something perceivable by the eye without depending on light,
just like the term "absence of light."
This category of substance has been defined; may it,
consisting of nine types, spread joy for the Lord of the Thirty-three, who likewise consists of ninefold nature.
Of the destroyer of Tripura, who is worthy of worship by the three worlds.
Thus ends the category of substance (*dravya*) in the illustrious *Mānamanohara*.
[The Section on Qualities] [1–4 Definition of Color, Taste, Odor, and Touch—
] 1) Direct perception is the means of valid cognition regarding color.
The subject of dispute arises at the time immediately following the production of the jar,
because it is a quality of the jar, like the conjunction with a jar that is commonly accepted.
Furthermore, "being a common quality" (*sāmānyaguṇatva*) cannot be the limiting condition (*upādhi*),

because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even the dimensions (*parimāṇa*) and other qualities residing in that [substance] would likewise be produced later. 2) The subject of dispute is an effect, because it is a specific quality of earth, like the color of a jar.
Furthermore, "being a property residing in an effect" (*kāryagatatva*) is not a valid limiting condition (*upādhi*),

because it does not pervade [the instances of] atomic conjunction (*paramāṇu-saṃyoga*), latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. 3) The subject of dispute (the effect) is [non-eternal], because, while being distinct from number, dimension, separateness, gravity, and latent impressions, it is a quality of earth, just like the conjunction of earthly atoms.
4) The subject of dispute possesses a specific quality produced by conjunction with fire,
because, while possessing an impermanent specific quality, it is eternal, like the self (ātman).
5) At the time when it serves as the substratum for a composite whole (avayavin), the subject of dispute does not produce color, because it is a substratum, like a water atom (jalāṇu).
6) The locus of qualities is distinct from the subject of dispute, its substratum, its destruction, and its effect,
because it possesses qualities and because it is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), like the self (*ātman*).
7) The nature of color (*rūpatva*) is inherent even in that which is not itself inherent.
Because it is a genus of form (*rūpajāti*), like existence (*sattā*).
8) The locus of dispute is not a substratum for multiple forms, because it is a whole (*avayavin*).
Like a white thread:
the subject of dispute is not the locus of blueness, because it is composed of yellow [threads].
The subject of dispute is not the locus of yellowness, because it is composed of blue, like yellow and like blue.
9) The subject of dispute is the locus of yellowness.
If it is argued that [the cloth] is yellow because it has begun as yellow, like [something already] yellow, we say no;
for this is sublated by the fact that two contradictory classes cannot coexist.
Otherwise, the subject of dispute, which is the locus of "cowness" (gotva), would also be the locus of "earthen-ness" (pārthivatva).

Furthermore, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is "the state of being color (rūpatva) that does not serve as the substratum for any genus distinct from 'yellowness' (pītatva), which is a sub-class of color."
By this, the claim that white color is only one is refuted, because its varying degrees are also observed.
10) It would have been said that it is a universal (sāmānya) because, while being eternal, it exists in multiple objects.
And because that [color] persists as long as the substance exists,
the perception of "red" among things produced by heating (*pākaja*) would be difficult to account for;
moreover, it is of many varieties.
Form (rūpa) is that which, being a quality, is perceivable by the eye alone among the two [senses], namely the eye and the tactile organ.
By this, taste, odor, and touch are also defined.
These should be understood as being variegated as well.
11) Taste is that which, being a quality (*guṇa*), is apprehended by the gustatory organ. 12) Odor is that which, being a quality, is apprehended by the olfactory organ.
Earth possesses touch because it is possessed of color, like fire.
The subject of dispute possesses touch, because it is the originator of a substance, like fire.
Between the senses of sight and touch, touch is the quality apprehended by the sense of touch alone.
[5–6. Examination of Number and Separateness—(I.
Proof of Unity and Unitary Separateness)] 1) It is the substratum of two qualities residing in different locations, which have contact as their non-inherent cause.
Because it possesses substantiality and because it possesses corporeality,
like the threads that initiate the production of a cloth;
nor is "possessing tangibility" a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
For it would follow that even [substances] such as jars, which possess tangibility, would be the substrata of those two kinds of qualities;
nor is "being the non-inherent cause of a substance" a valid limiting condition (*upādhi*), because the qualifier would be redundant.
Because if that which is without limiting conditions were to abandon its probandum, it would follow that it must abandon its own nature.
In that regard, among the two qualities present in space and so forth, one is oneness.
Furthermore, there is "one-ness-in-separation" (*apara-ekapṛthaktva*).
In other cases as well, those two are to be established for the very same reason stated previously.
2) Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is subject to dispute, is capable of being inherent in a single object that is an effect possessing an extension greater than its own.
Because they possess conjunction,
like the conjunction that initiates a triad;
3) atoms are the inherent causes of effects that subsist in more than one [atom] through conjunction.
Because of its atomicity, like a dyad (dvyaṇuka). 4) The subject of dispute, the composite whole (avayavin), has a common substratum with that which is fit to be its cause.
Because they possess the nature of being wholes,
like a dyad and like a double-threaded cloth;
and because color and the other qualities reside in a single substratum.
Because conjunction resides in two things,
and because [the object] is produced from three or four [atoms], there is no proving of what is already established.
By this very [argument], the establishment of dimension is also [achieved].
(II. Proof of non-unity and manifoldness) 1) That which is the subject of dispute is the substratum of cognition and the qualities of the body,
because it possesses substantiality and is an inherent cause, like the self (*ātman*).
Nor is "selfhood" (ātmatva) a limiting adjunct (upādhi),
because it would entail a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the Lord (īśvara). Here, "one" refers to the number one (anekatvasaṃkhyā).
Furthermore—[it refers to] manifold distinctness (*aneka-pṛthaktvam*).
2) Thus, number and distinctness, being established in this way, are also established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Indeed, there exists such usage as "one," "two," "three," and so forth.
Nor is this [distinction] without a basis,
for that would entail a contradiction of its status as a word.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that non-difference constitutes oneness, while the conjunction of differences constitutes multiplicity.
Is non-difference [of the cloth] identical with it, or distinct from it?
In the first case, the co-occurrence [of the expressions "one" and "cloth"] would be untenable.
Because they are synonyms.
If it is argued that in the second [case] this is the meaning of the term *dharmapada* as "conformity," what is the proof for this?
If it is argued that there is a conventional usage of non-difference regarding qualities and so forth, we say no;
for the mere existence of a convention does not establish the actual reality of the object, since such usage is frequently seen even in cases that are merely figurative (gauṇa).
If it is asked, "Since there is no sublation of the primary sense, how can it be secondary?", we say: no, because there is likewise no proof [for the primary sense].
Because the absence of an originating cause is clearly evident—

due to the non-existence of both inherent and non-inherent causes— the production [of sound] from the efficient cause alone can only be postulated once that [non-existence of other causes] has been established.
Because it is unperceived, that [distinction] is not established.

3) Even if the distinction and conjunction of the linguistic usages of "two-ness," "three-ness," and so forth—due to their inherence in distinct types of enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—do not lead to confusion, nevertheless, for children, cowherds, and others who have not attended to such distinct types of cognition, the usage "these two" is not based upon them; for the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) cannot be accounted for without the number two.
Since the dimension of an atom cannot be produced from the two eternal atomic dimensions, and since accumulation (pracaya) is not to be suspected [as a cause],
it must be stated that the dimension of the cause is not a proving factor.

In this case, because the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of possessing an intermediate excellence [of number] is present, and because that [excellence] does not initiate [the production of] magnitude even when it is produced by accumulation;
likewise, it is also produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
This is because [the cognition] conforms to the presence and absence of the knowledge that "this is one" and "this is one.

Nor can it be established as being due to manifestation (vyañjakatva), for we do not observe a fixed relationship between a manifestor and the manifested among objects that are grasped by the same sense organ, situated in the same location, and simultaneously connected to the sense organ, apart from the connection with the sense organ itself.
Therefore, there is an equality of conjunction with respect to duality.
4) Some say that duality is produced by cognition, because it is invariably perceived by a single cognizer.

For them, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to the prior non-existence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*); [this is avoided] if the qualification "provided it is a quality" (*guṇatve sati*) is added, as in the case of the will of the Lord (*īśvara-icchā*).
When the qualification "being an effect" is applied, this excludes cognitions such as those of waking.

Furthermore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since the non-perception of duality occurs in the absence of enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the destruction of that [cognition] is established as the cause of the destruction of duality.
The sequence of inference, however, is as follows: duality is inherent in an individual instance that is destroyed by the destruction of its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
Because it belongs to that same genus, like existence (*sattā*);
it inheres in the final cognition of pleasure of one practicing yoga, which is destroyed by the destruction of the body that serves as the instrumental cause for existence and so forth.
Thus, everything should be stated in the case of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).
[7. Examination of Dimension (parimāṇa)—

] 1) That which is the subject of dispute is the substratum of a quality residing in two things, distinct from the non-inherent cause of qualities residing in two things and from the non-eternal specific qualities,
because it is a substance, like a water atom.
Nor are "possessing tangibility" and "being corporeal" limiting conditions (upādhi),
because they deviate [from the probandum] in the case of the atoms of air and earth.
God is the substratum of qualities residing in [substances] other than the non-inherent causes of eternal specific qualities.
Because it possesses the nature of a self, like the individual soul (*jīva*).
When one intends to establish its eternity, unity, distinctness, and dimension, it should not be stated that it is a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
It should be understood as "not residing in two" (*adviṣṭha*), meaning it is devoid of the sub-class of qualities that reside in two things (*dviṣṭhaguṇatvāvāntarajāti*).
Otherwise, if [the object] were established as a single entity, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
2) Likewise, it must also be established by means of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*): there indeed exists this conventional usage, namely, "this is large," "this is large."
And here, the universal of "largeness" alone cannot be the cause,
because that would entail the impossibility of degrees of intensity;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of even the sweet taste.
Because the conventional usage [of "sweet"] is established by the generality of sweetness (*madhuratva-sāmānya*) alone, which resides in the substance.
3) Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), accumulation (*pracaya*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and dimension (*parimāṇa*) are the causes for the production of that [dimension].
That which is the subject of dispute is the substratum of a dimension distinct from atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*).
Because it is a substance.
That which is the subject of dispute has a dimension distinct from great dimension,
because it is a substance, like a jar and like an atom.
Furthermore, minuteness and magnitude are not the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) here,
because they would deviate in the case of color and other qualities;
and if [the reason] were qualified by "being a substance" (dravyatva), it would be redundant.
Furthermore, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the conventional usage of "short" and "long" serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the point that [dimension] perishes due to the destruction of its substrate, an ancient inference must be stated.
(4) Dimension is a quality belonging to a subordinate genus within the class of qualities that reside in that which has duality as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
[8. Definition of Conjunction—] 1) The subject of dispute is produced by a non-inherent cause, because it is an effect, like color.
Nor is there any deviation in the case of destruction.

Because the property of being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), when qualified by the condition "while being an entity" (bhāvatve sati), is unestablished (asiddha) in that case;
nor does even the suspicion of a limiting adjunct (upādhi) arise here,
for the cognition "two jars are conjoined" is perfectly clear.
Furthermore, since the theory of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been refuted, it should not be suspected that arising in contiguous locations is caused by that [momentariness].
Rather, the fact that karma and conjunction are the producers of that [arising] is established by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
For example, space is conjoined with the self (*ātman*).
Some say [the reason] is "because of being a substance" (*dravyatvāt*).
That is not correct, because [the properties of] possessing action (*kriyāvattva*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*), or priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatva*) serve as limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
The self (*ātman*) does not enter into conjunction with space (*ākāśa*).
[The reason] "because of being formless" [is not inconclusive], as it is like color;
nor is "not being a substance" a limiting condition (upādhi) here, because it does not pervade the similar instances (sapakṣa), since that [condition] is absent in space.
3) Its destruction occurs through both the destruction of its substratum and disjunction;
furthermore, the destruction of disjunction occurs through the destruction of its substratum and subsequent conjunction.
However, it has been stated that the destruction of conjunction occurs only through the destruction of its substratum and disjunction.

Since atoms and space are eternal, it is impossible for their conjunction to be destroyed by the destruction of its substratum. Furthermore, in the view that all beings are liberated, the manifestation of a contradictory quality is also difficult to establish.
Therefore, it is accepted that [the conjunction] is destroyed by the destruction of its efficient cause (*nimitta*).

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is an impermanent relation; it is a conjunction belonging to a sub-class of quality residing in the parts that produce a jar. [Now follows the definition of disjunction (*vibhāga*):]
1) Action (karma) is a non-inherent cause distinct from conjunction,
because, while being distinct from conjunction, it is a non-inherent cause, like color (rūpa).
Nor is "not being action" a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Because there is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of space and so forth;
even if the qualification "being an non-inherent cause" is added, there is still a deviation with respect to conjunction that initiates a mere conjunction;
and if the qualification "being distinct from conjunction" is added, it is redundant.
