Nor is there a contradiction in the subject matter [of the reason] based on the argument "because it is a non-inherent cause distinct from conjunction," since it is understood that conjunction itself is a non-inherent cause; for according to you, action is a non-inherent cause of action. Furthermore, in the first inference, there is no such thing as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Because that [momentum] is absent in slow motion, it is not established as something distinct;
and for you, even the formation (saṃskāra) is not established,
since the final action does not produce further action.
Because that very [distinction] is my own position.
Furthermore, this conventional usage of differentiation certainly exists,
and it is not without a basis.
Nor is the absence of conjunction the cause, because the cause exists only at the moment of the destruction of the conjunction;
nor does action possess causality in that regard.
Because it is not observed that qualities (guṇa) are destroyed by action (karman):
"The disputed conjunction (saṃyoga) is not destructible by action,
because it is a quality, like an admitted [quality]."
Nor is it correct to say that it is not destroyed by disjunction either, for that very reason;
because the pervasion is unestablished due to the non-establishment of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Or rather, its establishment [as a cause] is based on its very nature as the destroyer of that [effect],
since an effect cannot be established without a cause.
3) And it is of two kinds— distinguished as being born of action (*karmaja*) and born of disjunction (*vibhāgaja*).
The division under dispute does not have action as its non-inherent cause,
because it inheres in the same object as the action, like sound.
The subject of dispute is a substance distinct from the self, which is the substratum of qualities produced by division.
Because it is an eternal substance, like the self;
nor is "selfhood" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because that would lead to a deviation in the case of God (*īśvara*).
And because there is no pervasion in space.

4) Others, however, assert that at the time of the production of a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance, the action of the part does not initiate a disjunction from a location such as space, because it is an action.
That is incorrect, because one could also say: "Action initiates disjunction from the locus of space, because it is an action.
Therefore, disjunction cannot arise from the disjunction of its causes.
Furthermore, the argument that "the subject of dispute is disjoined by itself, because it is a substance" should be refuted as before.
5) Furthermore, its destruction occurs through both the destruction of the substratum and subsequent conjunction.

As for the claim that destruction results from subsequent conjunction, it should not be asserted even subsequently, because the very cognition [of such a cause] does not exist, despite the persistence of the cognition of disjunction.
Furthermore, since the employment of a word can be justified otherwise,
one cannot determine its primary meaning from mere hearing alone;
likewise, even for the word "separation" (vibhāga), there is no separate conventional designation [for it] in the absence of conjunction or the absence of connection.

Since we observe linguistic usage even regarding the prior non-existence of conjunction (*saṃyoga-prāgabhāva*), disjunction (*vibhāga*) is that which destroys conjunction while having the same substratum as the conjunction. [The definition of priority and posteriority: Priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) are defined as follows: [they are qualities produced by temporal or spatial distance].

1) The subject of dispute (vivādapada) produces qualities residing in multiple effects existing in atoms, or else atoms produce qualities residing in multiple effects existing in their products, because they possess corporeality (mūrtatva),
like an earth-atom or like a jar.
The subject of dispute produces qualities in the substance it initiates,
because, while being a substance itself, it is the initiator of a substance, like God;
the subject of dispute is produced by atoms.
It is the substratum of qualities that are not distinct from the cause of karma,
because it possesses form and lacks [intrinsic] qualities, like an earth atom.
Thus, its establishment is also achieved through the conventional usage of "prior" and "subsequent" regarding these two established entities.

Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the cognition of the lesser or greater degree of conjunctions resulting from the contact with the location of the sun’s revolution is established as the cause [of the perception of direction].
If it were merely a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), the same fault as previously mentioned should be understood to apply.
2) That which is the subject of dispute is the substratum of the qualities of non-hostile cognition and motion.
Because it is the substratum of the non-inherent cause of consciousness, like the self;
because those who do not possess the sense of hearing lack specific qualities;
and because "remoteness" (*paratva*) is a quality belonging to a sub-class of the genus "quality," produced by a quality residing in its own inherent cause, which is a product-substance.

Relative distance (*aparatva*) is a quality belonging to a sub-class of the genus "quality" (*guṇatva*), produced by its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—namely, the distance being acted upon—which possesses the same quality.
Its destruction results from the destruction of its cause. [12. Definition of Cognition (*buddhi*):]
1) It need not be stated that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) reside in the intellect, because this is established as a tenet common to all systems (sarvatantrasiddhānta).
If one were not to accept this, consequences such as contradiction with one's own words (svavacanavirodha) would follow.
The property of being knowledge (jñānatva) inheres in individual instances of mental perception belonging to ourselves and others,
because it is a genus of knowledge, like existence (sattā).

When the qualification "ourselves and others" is not intended, then [the property of] being an object of cognition (prameyatva) and so forth should be understood as establishing the perception of yogins.
If its perceptibility is not admitted, the admission of cognition itself becomes groundless,
since the conventional usage that postulates it can be established by the very cause of that [cognition].
Furthermore, there is no infinite regress.
Because the causal complex beginning with the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acts as a regulator;
and because, unlike color-form and so forth, manifestness (udbhūtatva) is not admitted to exist in cognition,
since only that which possesses such [manifestness] is perceptible.

2) It is not correct [to argue], according to the view of Prabhākara, that "the subject of dispute is not mental perception because it is a cognition," for in the case of the theory of universal liberation (*sarvamukti*), the example is unestablished; furthermore, even in any other case, there is no means of certain knowledge for Prabhākara’s [thesis] that the self is eternally one.

Furthermore, the objection that "in the cognition 'I know the jar,' one should postulate only a single cognition due to the parsimony of conceptualization (kalpanālāghava)"—and thus that the presentation of an *arthāpatti* (presumption) would be a fallacy—is incorrect;
for the opponent did not put forward the proof of multiplicity [of cognitions] as a premise.
3) Moreover, cognition is perceptible because it is a real entity (*vastu*), just like a jar.
Nor is "being non-cognition" a limiting adjunct (upādhi),
because for you, it is not established that all cognitions are perceptible;
furthermore, even if the negative particle denotes mutual absence (itaretarābhāva), the qualification would be redundant.
Its meaning is "the state of being distinct from cognition.
In that context, the word "cognition" (jñāna) serves no purpose;
for it is not the case that cognition is not a mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa).
It is not correct to say "because it is a cognition," for that reason is inconclusive;
nor is there the fault of infinite regress if [the cognition] is mental perception.
For those who maintain the theory of the admission of the capable (*yogyabhyupagamavāda*), that [error] is impossible and thus not a fault.
Therefore, cognition is mental perception. (1. Refutation of the Theory of Non-apprehension [*akhyātivāda*])
Now, some support the theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti) and state that the subject of dispute has silver as its object because it is a cognition of silver.
They, however, must be asked: what is this so-called "cognition of silver"?
1. Is "silver-cognition" (rajatajñāna) the cognition of silver? 2. Or is it both silver and its cognition? 3. Or is it a cognition that includes the verbal expression "silver"?
Or is it the cognition that serves as the cause for the activity of one desiring silver?
Not the first,
because the meaning of the genitive case cannot be anything other than the relationship between object and subject.
Because it is not distinct from the probandum;
nor is the second [alternative] valid, because it is unestablished for both parties.
Because cognition is formless (*nirākāra*),
the third [alternative] is also not tenable; for it is unestablished that the object of the mental mention (*ullekha*) functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) since it is possible for the word "silver" to be remembered even by means of the cognition of the preceding word, provided one possesses the mere memory produced by that cognition. Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable,

because for those who maintain that non-apprehension of the distinction is the cause [of error], even the cognition "this" which has the mother-of-pearl as its object would be a cause [of the erroneous cognition of silver], and thus there would be a deviation.
By this, the cognition "this is silver" is refuted,

because it does not fall outside the categories previously mentioned. Furthermore, as for those who assert that "the cognition under dispute is valid, because it is a cognition," [that too is refuted].
In this case, since the specific instance of knowledge admitted by both disputants is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

If one were to take as the subject merely that knowledge which produces [the action], as postulated on the grounds that the activity of one desiring silver would otherwise be inexplicable, there would be sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*),
because activity is produced by a knowledge of the means to achieve a desired object regarding an object identical to its own.
For you also have accepted that this [activity] proceeds from a correct understanding of the word;

in that case as well, if the mere apprehension of distinction (*viveka*) were the sole motivator, it would entail the collapse of the theory that words denote meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*).

This is because one observes a child’s own activity arising from the mere non-apprehension of distinction within himself, and thus infers that the activity of the middle-aged elder who acts immediately after the speech of the senior elder is likewise preceded by that same [mere non-apprehension of distinction].
Even though that specific cognition is not its cause, it is postulated there by the force of non-deviation at the moment preceding activity;
and for one who asserts that the word is the cause in that regard, there is a violation of accepted doctrine,
because such a postulation occurs solely through the fact of activity itself.
The eye produces a cognition that exceeds the cognition of visual objects,
because it is a sense organ, like the skin.
The subject of dispute [the sentence] causes the understanding of the syntactic connection between the objects recalled by its own constituent words.
[The collection of words] is [a means of knowledge] because it is a group of words possessing expectancy and proximity, like [the accepted examples].
Nor is "possessing semantic competency" (yogyatāvattva) a limiting condition (upādhi),
because words that are neither expected nor proximate do not produce cognition even when they possess semantic competency.
Because, due to expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*), the qualifier would be redundant if [the object] were already qualified;
therefore, there exists cognition that does not correspond to reality. (2. The divisions of invalid cognition:)
And that [non-perception] is divided, according to worldly convention, into the categories of certainty and uncertainty.
Uncertainty, moreover, is either non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) or doubt (*saṃśaya*).
False certainty is error (*viparyaya*).
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a certainty that touches upon two contradictory alternatives;
non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*) is a certainty that does not touch upon two contradictory alternatives,
since we too accept that the state of non-determination belongs to both doubt and non-ascertainment.
Furthermore, since Bhaṭṭa Bhāsarvajña has accepted the internal subdivisions we have mentioned, there is no disagreement between us and him; thus, this matter is not elaborated upon here.
As for *tarka* (hypothetical reasoning), it is nothing other than what is already subsumed under the definition of "non-determination" (*anadhyavasāya*).
[3. Definition of Direct Perception: The eye is the producer of a cognition distinct from the conceptual cognition produced by the eye, because it is a sense organ, like the mind.
The subject of dispute is perceptible, because it is a real entity and because it is an object of cognition, like a jar.
Some maintain that the presence of the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
That is not so, because that too is established.
This [objection] is untenable,
because its object is sublated.
If it is argued that this is because the object is not connected with the external sense-faculties,
since the mind lacks independence regarding external objects,
otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would indeed be a subverting factor; however, by way of its specific restriction, it will also be a proving factor.
The merit born of yoga, established by the scriptural statement "the Self is to be known," has as its fruit such qualities as omniscience.
Nor is it correct to say that he is not a fashioner of dharma, because without him [dharma] would be impossible;
for even among those possessed of yoga, birth in a distinguished family— which is conducive to the knowledge of reality— is impossible without a specific excellence of dharma.
As the Blessed One himself has said: "The one fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous" (Gītā 6.41).

For the sake of generating knowledge in those such as ourselves, [the sense organ] acts according to the circumstances by depending upon conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) with its object.
However, *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in that which is conjoined) is not something other than the combination of conjunction and inherence.
Otherwise, it would follow that it is a distinct category of entity; thus, this is not elaborated further.
Eternal divine cognition is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is a non-inferential knowledge of things as they truly are.
(4. Definition of inferential cognition)
(4.1 This might be the case—) if it is asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for inference?", we reply: "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For indeed, there arises the cognition, "The mountain possesses fire," as is the thought of someone situated at a great distance.
Nevertheless, do not say, "How is its nature as an inference (anumititva) understood by him? for the same difficulty applies even in the case of perception (pratyakṣa).
Nor should it be asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the inference of that [perception's] cause?"
Is it merely the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is established,
such that there could be a question regarding its specific nature?

And as for its establishment, whether it is by this very means of valid cognition— also known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— which enters into the causal complex of perception, or by another, this is quite trivial.
(4.2 The Nature of Pervasion) — Now, it may be objected that the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) being asserted by you is untenable, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not exist.
Or, [one might argue] it is because [the pervasion] cannot be known even when established; [we reply:
no, for pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a relation that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*). If it is asked, "What, then, is a limiting condition?"
When two things are never observed to coexist in the absence of a third, that third thing is the *vyabhicāra* (deviation) of one with respect to the other,
and it is the *upādhi* (limiting condition) in that case;
or alternatively, it is that which pervades only the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Or, it is that which pervades the probandum while also pervading the probans.
It is of two kinds: the positive adjunct (*anvayopādhi*) and the negative adjunct (*vyatirekopādhi*). Both of these are further divided into those that are suspected and those that are certain.
In the argument, "The subject of dispute (the self) is devoid of existence because it is a genus, like the category of existence," the nature of existence itself is suspected to be the *upādhi*.
In the argument, "The Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice is a means to sin because it is an act of violence," being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*) is determined to be the *upādhi*;
for even though there is no invariable concomitance with the probans (*hetu*), the *upādhi* is observed to follow along with the probandum (*sādhya*) in cases such as the theft of gold.
In the argument "The earth and so forth are without an agent because they are not produced by an embodied being, like space," the condition (*upādhi*) of "not being produced" is established;
for there is no evidence to justify the assumption that the qualified [condition] is the actual probans.
In the argument "Every effect is preceded by eternal effort because it is an effect, unlike space," the condition is "not being preceded by effort."
The inclusion of a qualification in the probandum (*sādhya*) is a defect in a positive inference (*anvayin*).

However, in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), since it is the absence [of that qualification] which serves as the means of proof, the qualification has no utility as a delimiter; thus, the qualification is redundant.
Like the pungency inherent in smoke, this is indeed a defect.

By this, the case of a suspected *upādhi* (limiting condition) is also to be inferred. Furthermore, since the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is intended only in the context of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), even in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it remains identical to the positive case; thus, the final definition is also applicable there.
Nor is it impossible to know the absence of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
because for those [adjuncts] that have never been perceived, their status as an adjunct is untenable due to their non-existence even at the very first moment of perception;
for a *japā* flower that does not exist cannot function as a limiting adjunct.
The non-existence of those [atoms] is determined by the non-perception of their fivefold aggregates;
however, the attribution of supersensible adjuncts cannot occur even when mere inference exists,
because it lacks a basis.
Regarding the specific types of inference, however, that which is accepted by the proponent and the opponent must be refuted by defining the true nature of the specific categories of those terms.

(4.3 *Parārthānumāna*— ) In this context, *parārthānumāna* (inference for the sake of others) consists of a verbal formulation comprising the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*nidarśana*), the application (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*).
In this regard, because worldly linguistic usage proceeds according to the order of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*),

and for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) as well as because the knowledge of the locus (*āśrayajñāna*) is required first, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) comes first;
immediately after that, the statement of the reason (*hetu*).
Because it is the substratum of that [inference].

When the mere establishment of the cause is accomplished and there arises a desire to know its specific nature, the statement of the reason alone is made by considering the requirements of the inquiry.
Subsequently, when there is a desire to know the property (*dharma*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is investigated because it is required.

Immediately following that, there is the statement of the conclusion (*nigamana*), which serves to demonstrate the unity of all the preceding statements and to proclaim the establishment of the desired probandum (*sādhya*).
For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced;
whatever is produced is impermanent, as for example, a jar."
And sound is a product;
therefore, sound is impermanent.
The statement of the thesis is the proposition (*pratijñā*).
The statement of the reason is the *apadeśa*; the statement of the example is the *udāharaṇa*;
and the statement of the reason immediately following the statement of the example is the *upanaya*.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) together with its reason (*sahetuka*), following immediately after the application (*upanaya*).
If it is argued that the conclusion need not be employed because its meaning is already understood, we say no;
for that [omission] would constitute a flaw [in the argument].
Otherwise, only the reason itself would need to be employed,
because for those who are wise, the specific object [of the thesis] is understood from the sense of the matter alone.
(4.4 The Doctrine of Two Members)
We do not consider that to be a fault, because it constitutes an excess of speech that is not applicable to the proof (*sādhana*).
For the opponent has indeed expressed a desire to know the proof by asking, "What is the means of valid cognition? (*kiṃ pramāṇam*).
In that regard, as many factors as are required to constitute a qualified proof must be stated;
and those factors are precisely two: pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
For there is nothing further than that which serves as a factor for engagement [in action]. What is there to be known that would exceed it?
Because the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy is included within the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, since two types of unconditional inference cannot coexist in a single instance,
or if they did, who could prevent a thing from having a dual nature?
For if that which is unconditional were to abandon its probandum, it would follow that it must abandon its very essence.
This being the case regarding the two-fold nature [of the reason],

only two statements must be made for the purpose of establishing it; for its establishment is achieved by the statement of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), which expresses that specific qualification.
Therefore, whatever is an effect is impermanent, like a jar; and sound is an effect— this is the positive concomitance (anvayi).
Whatever is eternal is unproduced, like space;
and sound is produced—this is the negative inference (*vyatirekin*).
Therefore, only two members [of the syllogism] should be employed.

Another [type of reason], the "positive-negative" (anvayavyatirekin), is not accepted, because there is no evidence for the combined [positive and negative] being the cause when the inference is established by one alone. Inference (anumiti) is the indirect experience produced by invariable concomitance (avinābhāva); the means most effective in establishing that is inference (anumāna).
That which lacks the defining characteristics [of a valid inference] and resembles it is a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*).
(4.5 Fallacious Reasons) And that is divided into the categories of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The unestablished (*asiddha*) is that which does not reside in the subject (*pakṣa*) whose nature is yet to be determined,
such as "sound is impermanent because it is visible.
This [unestablished reason] is further divided into that which is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*) and that which is unestablished for one or the other (*anyatarāsiddha*).
A reason (*hetu*) that exists only in the similar class (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), as in:
"Sound is eternal because it is a product.
For a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) consists in making known the lack of probative power (*asādhakatva*).

The contradictory reason (*viruddha*) functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*) by virtue of its being related to the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) in a manner that is free from any limiting condition (*anaupādhika*).

If it is objected: "But does not the tendency to lead to the opposite of the probandum sometimes deviate [from the truth], such that being free from limiting conditions would be insufficient? Therefore, this specific qualification is not a valid criticism"—[we reply: no.
That is not so; for in the case of debate (*jalpa*) and discussion (*vāda*), one must set aside the opponent's proof and state the proof for one's own position.
Therefore, for the sake of brevity, a qualified presentation is made;
however, no other proof need be stated at all.

In the case of cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), however, one should primarily point out the presence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and its nature as an obstacle to the arising of inference is the defect (*dūṣaṇa*). An inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) is that which is known to exist in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence.
And that [reason] is both certain and doubtful.
What is it? "Sound is impermanent."

The reason "because it is an object of cognition" is certain [as a fallacious probans]. The reason "the mind is all-pervading, because it is a substance always devoid of touch" is suspected [of being fallacious],
because it possesses an extraneous condition (upādhi).

(4.6 Pseudo-example [dṛṣṭāntābhāsa]:)— The pseudo-example, moreover, consists of that which lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikala), that which lacks the probans (sādhanavikala), the failure to state the pervasion (vyāptyakathana), the statement of a reversed pervasion (viparītavyāptikathana), and that which lacks a locus (āśrayahīna).

Examples of the similar instance (sādharmyodāharaṇa) and the dissimilar instance (vaidharmyodāharaṇa) involving the absence of the property to be proven, the absence of the probans, the failure to state the pervasion, and the statement of a reversed pervasion have been set forth by Praśastapāda.
They are not elaborated upon;
however, that which is devoid of both does not exist,
because it is not distinct from those cases where either the probandum or the probans is absent.
For there is no such combined refutation as "inconclusiveness due to being stated after the time has passed.
[5. Examination of the Existence of Ārṣa Knowledge: If it is asked, "What is the proof for the existence of ārṣa [knowledge]?"
We say that it is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There exists, indeed, for those who disagree, a certain intuition (*pratibhā*) which is non-discrepant with respect to some object.
Because it apprehends an object not previously cognized, its status as a direct experience (*anubhūti*) is established.
Nor does there remain any such thing as "validity" (prāmāṇya) apart from this that would need to be established; nor is it the case that non-contradiction with the object does not exist,
because there is no sublation (bādhaka).
Nor is there a lack of correspondence with the object due to its being a mental flash (*pratibhā*),
because it is immediate (*aparokṣa*);
otherwise, it would follow that even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) lacks correspondence with the object.

If it is argued that inference alone is weak because its object is sublated— since the object apprehended by that cognition is established as being real through perception which grasps its non-discrepancy with knowledge, and through the unobstructed activity preceded by that [perception], and thus possesses causal efficacy—
then the resolution is the same.
If it is asked, "Even though there is no difference in their being intuitive flashes (*pratibhā*), how can one be consistent (*saṃvādin*) while the other is inconsistent (*visaṃvādin*)?", we say: No;
for even though there is no difference in their being immediate (*aparokṣatva*), why would one perception (*pratyakṣa*) be consistent while another is not?
If it is argued that this is due to a distinct intermediate class [of cognition],
let the validity of intuition (*pratibhā*) be equal [to that of perception and inference].
If it is further argued that, nevertheless, it must be included within the former two, we say no.
Because it does not depend on invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), it is not included within inference;
and because it is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it is not perception. If it is asked, "But how is this [knowledge] beyond the senses?"—
If it is asked how inference, too, is non-perceptual—
on the grounds that it arises in the absence of sensory activity—
this [reason] is the same [for both].
If it is argued that there is an operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the same [objection] applies.
If it is argued that because it arises from a specific merit (*dharma*) it is included within yogic perception, we say no, because its arising from a specific merit is unestablished.
Because the state of being produced solely by a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The *ārṣa* [perception] is a correct experience of the imperceptible that is independent of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Memory (*smaraṇa*) is that which is produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is identical to its own.
There is no disagreement regarding the status of valid cognition (pramāṇa) when it corresponds to reality, because even others admit that it is a correct experience (samyaganubhava),
and even logicians do not deny that it possesses the nature of knowledge corresponding to reality (yathārthajñānatva).
Therefore, the ancient teachers [held that] valid cognition (*pramā*) is correct experience;
the moderns [hold that] valid cognition is knowledge that accords with reality (*yathārtha-jñāna*).
And this alone is the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

Otherwise, its inclusion among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be inconsistent; for in common worldly usage, there is no difference in meaning between the terms *pramiti* (valid cognition) and *vidyā* (knowledge). Therefore, the means of valid cognition are fourfold.
((Thus, there is a fourfold set of means of knowledge: scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), perception (*pratyakṣa*), and oral testimony (*aitihya*).

(6. Determining the inclusion of verbal testimony (*śabda*) within inference (*anumāna*))—Now, if it is argued that there are indeed other means of knowledge besides these, such as verbal testimony and so forth:
If it is argued that the cognition of the meaning arises from the sentence "There are five fruits on the riverbank" because [the objects] are not unestablished, then let it be considered:
what here possesses the status of being the cause? It is not perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because the meaning is indistinct;
because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) for inference.
For in the sentence "There are five fruits on the riverbank," there is no invariable relationship between the riverbank and the fruits.
Because that [reliability] is absent in the speech of one who is not authoritative (*anāpta*).

If the qualification "provided there is authoritativeness" is added, then since authoritativeness is established only by the prior establishment of the object, the meaning of the sentence remains unestablished;
for authoritativeness belongs only to one who possesses correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
This is incorrect,
because the fact that it was spoken by a specific person is taken precisely as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*);
and since what was spoken by him is also established through inference, there is no lack of probative force (*aprayojakatā*).
But where there is some deviation even in that which has been stated by him,
there the qualification "provided it is distinct from that" must also be added; for it is the qualified [reason] that functions as the means of proof through the power of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
But where there is a locus of deviation, there is no certainty regarding the object; rather, there is only doubt.

Even by this much, since the engagement of worldly people in action is established through doubt alone regarding their purpose, [one might ask]: "If the Veda lacks the quality of being composed by a specific person, how can there be inference [regarding its authority]? If this is asked:
In that case, since the status of being spoken by a reliable authority (*āptoktatva*) would also be absent, it would follow that the Veda lacks validity;
nor is there intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) for the Veda, because it is produced by causes distinct from those common to both correct and false cognitions.
For instance, valid cognition (pramā) is produced by causes distinct from those common to both correct and erroneous cognitions,
because it is an effect, just like invalidity (apramāṇya).

Even when there is certain knowledge, correctness (*samyaktva*) is not always determined; for even if certainty exists, it may still be a subject of doubt, like an invalid cognition (*apramā*). The effect under dispute...
[The Veda] arises from a cognition produced by the Veda,
because it is an effect, like a jar.
Although there is no difference in their being created by Īśvara, the words of the Buddha and others lack authority due to the presence of adventitious defects.
Because the Buddha and others are not authoritative,
the meaning of the Veda is to be known through a means of valid cognition that is independent of the Veda, since it is an object of knowledge, like a jar.

The meaning of the Veda is cognizable by means of a sentence composed upon a basis consisting of a cognition that does not depend on the Veda itself, because it is an object of knowledge, like anything commonly agreed upon;
and every study of the Veda is preceded by the teacher’s own study.
Just as the current study [of the Veda] follows from the commonality of the study of the Vedas.

(Ślokavārttika, Vākya 366) Furthermore, regarding that [point], if it were merely a matter of being preceded by the study under a teacher, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*);
for even Brahman, who is a particular kind of living being, remembers the Vedas experienced in another kalpa, like one who has awakened from sleep.
Nor does it follow that [the Veda] would lack a creator simply because its stream has been interrupted,
for we admit that its authorship in that case belongs to one who is independent of any knowledge of a sentence similar to the one being uttered.
However, if one intends to mean authorship by an independent person, then the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).
Even if one accepts the subject (pakṣa) as admitted by both disputants, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā);
in the other case, however, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi),
because it would be equally possible to apply this [argument] to the study of the Mahābhārata and so forth.
Is this [reason]— "because its author is not remembered while its tradition remains unbroken"— belonging to me,
or to you, or is it common to anyone at all?
In the first, third, and fourth [reasons], there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*);
in the second, however, there is inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*).

For this very reason, in my inference... [one line lost in the manuscript] ...otherwise, because it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), "not being an effect" (*akāryatva*) would be a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
(8. The inclusion of the means of valid cognition *upamāna* within *anumāna*:
But *upamāna*, such as [the cognition] "my cow is similar to this," when one perceives a gavaya that resembles a cow, is indeed nothing but *anumāna*.
If it is asked, "How so? [the answer follows:]

For there indeed first arises the inference: "There is similarity to a cow in the gavaya," because a recurring property existing in the gavaya is fit to be grasped by perception, and it is logically possible for even that which is brought forward by another means of knowledge to function as a qualifier.
Alternatively, my cow is similar to this one,
because it delimits it through its own similarity,
like a brother and sister.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the similarity to a *gavaya* could not be apprehended.
According to the view of perception, since the relationship between qualifier and qualified is seen to be a matter of convention (*kāmacāra*), one infers the cow as delimited by similarity.

Then, regarding the connection between the name and the named object, the person—having clarified the individual through the application of the logical method (*nyāya*) concerning what was previously doubted—subsequently understands the meaning of the sentence as it has been ascertained.

When it is determined that similarity alone is the denotation of the word *gavaya*—based on the consideration that otherwise there would be the consequence of non-usage for those who have not perceived [the animal], and based on the impossibility of the trustworthy person (āpta) speaking otherwise when his question was found to be inconsistent with having no basis—the very same sentence conveys that the word *gavaya* has "gavayatva" (the state of being a gavaya) as its primary cause [of application].
Thus: the word *gavaya* denotes *gavayatva*.

Because, in the absence of any other mode of signification (*vṛtti*), it is employed by experts as a term based on a specific occasion (*naimittika-pada*), just as the word "cow" (*go*) [denotes] cowness (*gotva*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), for you yourself have admitted the non-existence of any other mode of signification.
Otherwise, inference would not function due to the absence of a supporting *tarka* (reasoning). [The subject] under dispute is the ground for the application of the word "gavaya."
"Because it possesses a specific genus, like 'cowness' (gotva) as distinguished [from other genera].
(9. Description of presumptive testimony [arthāpatti] as being inference: Presumptive testimony is also inference.
For instance, even when one perceives an object that is otherwise inexplicable without the knowledge of a relation, the attainment of valid cognition (*pramiti*) occurs;
however, once the relation is known, what arises for you is merely inference (*anumāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the conflict between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when one has scope and the other lacks it, the one with scope undergoes a restriction of its object—this is the case for one who has observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For one who perceives the non-perception of the person in the house as being without scope, and perceives the statement regarding his being alive— which is contradictory to that— as having scope,
the resulting cognition that the object of that statement is external is indeed an inference (*anumāna*).
Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), however, does not even rise to the level of a possibility.

Since there is no absence of the non-occurrence of a sentence in the absence of another sentence— for the sentence "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day" is not unintelligible without the sentence "He eats at night"—
and since verbal expectancy is fulfilled by a word alone (not by perception or other means),
[one might argue]: "The word *pacati* ('he cooks') is not rendered expectant by perception and so forth, but rather by the word *odana* ('rice')"— if this is said, it is not so.
If it is argued that in this sentence there is an absence of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) because the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) are complete,
and that "corpulence is inexplicable without eating because it is the effect of eating," [we reply:]
In that case, there is no absence of expectancy;
rather, there would be an absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
And even that [absence] does not exist here, for it would only occur in the case of a prohibition against eating at all three times of the day.
For one who has not eaten does not remain fat even for a moment.
As for the prohibition of eating at all three times of the day, let the inference of the cause of eating at night—based on the specific effect [of corpulence]—proceed freely;
there is no room for the postulation of a separate scriptural statement regarding the night.
If it is argued that, in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), the postulation of the word "rice" (*odana*) there itself constitutes presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*),

even in that case, it is the meaning alone that is being postulated. Furthermore, if one maintains the restrictive rule that "even when implied by a word, it must be the word itself [that is postulated]," there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, such a word [is understood] through its pervasion (*vyāpti*) precisely by way of a specific relation; thus is that [relation] postulated.
Furthermore, what is this so-called "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*)?
If it is said to be the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), then from where does that arise?
If it is argued that this is because the word and its meaning do not terminate [in their denotation], then this is simply an acceptance of what is desired (iṣṭāpatti).
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the disappearance of words.
Because it is accepted as such, its inclusion within inference from verbal testimony has been asserted.
(10. The inclusion of non-apprehension within perception—)
Non-existence is perceptible, because it is an object of cognition, like a pot;
nor is the absence of a connection between the sense organ and its object a subverting factor [against its perception].
If it is asked, "What is the fault if even that which is unrelated [to the senses] were perceptible?"—
if you say, "It would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)," then the non-perception of the perceptible (dṛśyānupalabdhi) will serve as the remedy for that.
Nor should it be said that such a mere [absence] possesses causality,
for it would follow that even a blind person would perceive the absence of yellowness in a white cloth;
for the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is not necessarily perceived by the very same sense organ [by which the locus is perceived].
Therefore, the locus itself must be apprehended, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of apprehending the absence of touch in space;
for we admit that even when a temple is being remembered, there is a cognition of Devadatta’s absence therein.
The detailed discussion may be found in the *Nyāyalakṣmīvilāsa*, so I shall desist here.
(13–14 Examination of Pleasure and Pain) Pleasure is perceived through direct perception, as is evidenced by the observation of the conventional usage, "I am happy."

Moreover, the mere absence of suffering is not itself happiness, because we observe the conventional usage of the term "happiness" even when suffering is present— for instance, in the case of one who is tormented by heat and has half his body submerged in a cool lake, who possesses the thought, "I am happy. Furthermore, the absence of certain sufferings exists even for a denizen of hell.
And that [happiness] is not eternal,
for otherwise the employment of specific causes would be rendered useless;
happiness is that which, when being known, is pervaded by an activity free from limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

Thus, "suffering" should be defined as follows: suffering is that which is to be abandoned without qualification. (15–17 [An Examination of Desire, Aversion, and Effort]) Action is produced by qualities that have effort as their instrumental cause.
Because it is an action, like a pot; furthermore,
the quality that is the cause of the action, which is the subject of dispute, is produced by cognition,
because it is a quality that is the cause of an action.

Because each respective cause—namely, the cognition of pleasure or pain—is of a distinct genus (*vaijātya*), the effect is also of a distinct genus; thus, desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and volition (*prayatna*) are established.
Among these, both desire and volition are both eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*), just like cognition (*buddhi*).
Desire belongs to a sub-genus of quality (*guṇatva*) produced by a cognition of pleasure caused by the qualities that serve as the causes of action.
Hatred is a quality belonging to a sub-class of *guṇatva* (the property of being a quality) produced by the cognition of suffering caused by the factors of action;
effort is a quality belonging to a sub-class of *guṇatva* indicated by the purposeful activity perceptible to people like us.
(18–20: Definition of gravity, fluidity, and viscidity)

(1. Gravity—) The subject of dispute is produced by a non-inherent cause, because it is an action, like that which is commonly accepted; furthermore, that which is under dispute is imperceptible to us and others.
Because of its heaviness;
for example, like a jar [which falls when released].
Heaviness is a quality belonging to a sub-class of the genus "quality" (guṇatva) which serves as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of the first instance of falling.
(2. Fluidity—) Flowing is produced by a non-inherent cause, because it is an effect, like a jar; thus, fluidity is established.
And by perception:
fluidity is a quality belonging to a sub-class of the genus "quality," having as its non-inherent cause the initial flow;
the fiery atoms are the substrata of fluidity.
Because it possesses the nature of a material atom, like an earth-atom; nor are heaviness and possession of taste limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
because they are absent in a jar where the probandum is present.

Nor is this [moisture] qualified by atomhood (*paramāṇutva*) the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it is not a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpaka*); for even though the probandum is established in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like, [moisture] is absent there.
(3 Moisture: Water is the substratum of a quality that distinguishes its own locus from others by means of a sub-class of the genus "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*).
Because it possesses taste,
like the earth; and "earth-ness" is not a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Because it does not pervade the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

This being the case, viscidity (*sneha*) is also established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Viscidity is that which, while being perceptible by both sight and touch, distinguishes its own substratum by means of a subordinate genus within the category of quality (*guṇatva*).
(21. Definition of *saṃskāra*—) (1.
*vega*: Velocity)—That which is the substratum of the non-inherent cause of motion not directed toward an object of aversion is [possessed of] velocity, because it is an atom, like an earth-atom.
Nor is "possessing form" (rūpitva) a limiting condition (upādhi),
because it deviates in the case of light;
nor is "atomicity of the possessed form" (rūpy-aṇutva) the determining factor.
Because it does not pervade the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Since the production of a dyad composed of fire-atoms (taijasa-dvyaṇuka) possessing obstructed fluidity is also possible,
the qualification "being an atom" (paramāṇutve sati) would be redundant for the purpose of excluding that case.
And that momentum, when the substance is perceptible, is grasped by perception itself, because there is the cognition "it moves with momentum.
(2. *Sthitisthāpaka*—)
The atoms under dispute are the substrata of qualities residing in multiple locations due to having non-inherent causes of action,

because they possess touch, and because they possess non-auditory, non-eternal specific qualities— just like a bowstring, a drumstick, and the self. Otherwise, there would be no re-circling of branches and so forth that have been pulled out and released.
That which is the subject of dispute is the substratum of a residual impression (*saṃskāra*) exceeding [the force of] velocity,
because it possesses non-auditory, non-eternal specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*),
like the self (*ātman*); thus is established the existence of the elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).
The *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) is a *saṃskāra* belonging to a sub-class of qualities distinct from [the *saṃskāra*] that is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of upward motion.
(3. *Bhāvanā*—) The existence of *bhāvanā* is established because memory would otherwise be inexplicable;
for the prior experience has long since passed away.
Impression (*bhāvanā*) is a subordinate class of quality (*guṇa*) that produces a cognition having the same object as the impermanent cognition that produced itself.
(22–23: Examination of Dharma and Adharma) (1.
Dharma: Sacrifice (*yāga*) possesses an intermediate operation capable of producing heaven.
Otherwise, the established relationship of means and end between the sacrifice and heaven could not be maintained.
For it is understood that heaven possesses the status of an end by virtue of being the object of desire,
and that the sacrifice possesses the status of a means and must be performed by the force of the injunction.

Nor should it be argued that the relationship of means and end between a momentary sacrifice and a heaven occurring at a later time is untenable without an intermediate operation, and that this establishes the existence of the *apūrva* in the interim; for others maintain that the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice and heaven is not understood from the scriptural statement regarding the *apūrva*,
due to a lack of semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
Therefore, they assert that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) itself denotes the *apūrva*, while its derivation [of meaning] is established through both worldly usage and the Veda;
for even in the world, one observes the use of the optative suffix in reference to an action to be performed (*kārya*).

In that regard, according to the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), it is accepted that cognition occurs even without [the object's] fitness (*yogyatā*). Furthermore, in the context of optional rites (*kāma-adhikāra*), since that very thing which is a cause with respect to the fruit is accepted as the object (*viṣaya*) with respect to the injunction (*niyoga*),
otherwise there would be no distinction between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites.

Dharma is a quality of the self that is beyond the senses of those such as ourselves, and it consists of the genus of actions prescribed by injunctions; (and adharma is its opposite)—as is understood from the fact that the hundredfold torment [of hell] is to be accomplished [as a result], according to the Vedic text: "He who raises a weapon against a Brāhmaṇa, let him be tormented with a hundred [strokes]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.10.2).
Since the act of threatening has long since passed, its status as a means [to the result] is not directly possible; therefore, there must be an intermediate apūrva.
Because it is conjoined with the state of being unrighteous (*adharmatva*), it is "unrighteous" (*adharma*).
(24. Definition of the Word)

Sound is a quality (guṇa), because it is the locus of a genus that is perceived by that very [faculty] among the external sense organs which perceives a composite whole (avayavin), like odor. If sound were a substance (dravya),...
There must be some specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), otherwise perceptibility would be untenable, because the perceptibility of a substance is dependent upon the perceptibility of its specific quality.
If it is argued that sound is a substance because it is perceived through direct contact with the sense organ, like a jar, we say no; for the qualification is redundant.
Indeed, for those who maintain the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), there is no contact obstructed by color and other qualities.
Now, as for the argument "because it is apprehended by a sense organ connected to itself," even so, the term *indriya* (sense organ) is redundant;

nor is there any exclusion [of unwanted objects] by the terms *sva* (self) or *grāhya* (apprehended), because in your own system, you do not admit a relation (*sambandha*) for that which is not a substance (*adravya*).
Because "conjunction" (saṃyoga) and "relation" (sambandha) are synonymous, and because [the term "relation"] is used metaphorically in other cases;
otherwise, there would be a logical deviation (vyabhicāra), since even color (rūpa), by virtue of its relation characterized as "fitness" (yogyatā), is not directly perceived despite being related.
The reason "because of being related" is inconclusive for the opponent. [For example:
Sound is not a quality, because it is audible.
If it is argued that it is like "sound-ness" (śabdatva), we say no;
for this [sound-ness] is similar [to the subject] by virtue of not being a substance (adravyatva).
Furthermore, for you, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to the number residing in sound.
Sound is a quality, because, while being distinct from the self, it is the locus of a genus that is perceived by a sense organ as eternal, like pleasure.
Sound is impermanent.
Because it is a specific quality of a sense faculty (*indriya*), like the color-form residing in the eye;
nor is there a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on [the claim] that it resides in space alone, like the magnitude (*mahattva*) of that [space].
Because there is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of its own conjunction, like a jar destroyed in a portion of space.

Against the Bhāṭṭa, [the argument is]: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is the locus of a genus that is perceived only by that which does not perceive a composite whole while being itself non-material, like odor. And as for the claim that "sound is eternal,"...
"Because, while being distinct from the specific qualities of the self, it is perceived by one of the senses as something eternal"—
this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the absence of suffering.
It remains so even if the qualification "while possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavattve sati*) is added.
Because even in that case, the [opponent’s] own position accepts a universal (*jāti*);
as it has been said:
"Or rather, because this [object] is grasped by cognitions of both inclusion and exclusion..."
Therefore, let it be understood that [the self] is bound by the cow and so forth, because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*).
(Ślokavārttika, Abhāva 9) Thus,
[the reason] is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for the opponent,
because the conjunction of ether and air— which is graspable by the sense organs through its capacity— is likewise [non-existent].
The qualification "such as ours" is redundant,
and there is also a deviation [from the rule] due to [the case of] echoes;
this being established, even by means of perception it is proven that sound perishes, because of the cognition [that arises].

Sound is a specific quality of space. That which lacks the status of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) in the absence of another genus, or that which possesses the state of having another genus residing only in efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa), is a quality.
Alternatively, it is the state of being a distinct genus existing even in that which lacks both inherent and non-inherent causes.
[The Section on the Category of Action] 1) The first conjunctions and disjunctions are produced by non-inherent causes.
Because it is an effect, like a jar; thus is action established.
And that [action] is perceptible.
Because it is an object of cognition, like a jar.
The subject of dispute is distinct from the conjunction with the sense organ and is the apprehender of the non-inherent cause of conjunction,
because it is a sense organ that apprehends a substance, like the mind.
The example [in the argument] "karma is not directly perceived because it is an action" is unestablished; furthermore,
by the qualification "one who is not a yogi," the pervasion (vyāpti) is unestablished.
Because [the opponent] does not accept [such a cause],
conjunction and disjunction would be established from that very cause alone; furthermore, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that action (*karman*) is unestablished.
2) And that [action] belongs to a class distinct from other [qualities] such as infinite number,
because it is the cause of cognitions such as "falling" and "lifting.
Alternatively, action is of a class identical to the non-inherent cause of the first disjunction, or rather, it is that which is fit to be the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions.
By this, the distinction of action from all qualities that apprehend difference is established.
[Section on the Category of Universals:

Although it is argued that the existence of a universal is not tenable because a cognition of a single form would be inexplicable among distinct things without a single underlying cause, [this is not so].
Even when such a perception occurs, because there is disagreement regarding it,

it is not correct to say that "this is established" simply because there is no dispute while the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is in operation; for one could just as well say that "this is sublated."
Nevertheless—
because the cause is established, because conceptualization also possesses differentiation,
and because exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is likewise distinct, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Therefore, genus exists. (1 Regarding existence— ) The substance that is the subject of dispute has a homogeneous inherent cause, because it is an inherent cause, like clay.
Nor is "possessing tangibility" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it would involve a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in your view regarding the ultimate composite (*antyāvayavin*).
For us, however, once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established and existence is apprehended, the proof holds even elsewhere.

Because it functions as a destroyer of pervasion (*vyāpti*), its status as a fallacy (*dūṣaṇa*) occurs precisely at the time of [establishing] pervasion; for the determination of the subject (*pakṣa*) and other factors occurs subsequent to the establishment of pervasion. Furthermore, setting aside mere existence, the presence of the *upādhi* is found even in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) within ultimate composite wholes (*antyāvayavin*).
(2 *Substantiality*—
) That which is the subject of dispute possesses a genus that resides in color and is accompanied by touch,

because it is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), like a jar. Here, since the very object of the dispute possesses such a nature, there is no fault in the inclusion of the qualification in the probandum (*sādhya*).
Otherwise, it would suffice to prove only that which has been [already] disclosed:
earth-ness (pṛthivītva) possesses a genus that does not reside in water, as it is the subject of the dispute.
Because it possesses the nature of odor, like a jar; [and] because it possesses the nature of water— [the subject under dispute] possesses a genus that does not reside in earth,
because it possesses weight, like a jar.
(5. Luminosity—) That which is the subject of dispute possesses a genus that does not reside in what is non-hot, because it is hot, like a lamp.
To prove that [the genus] does not reside in air, one should state "because it is possessed of color" (*rūpitvāt*).
(6 Vāyutva— ) That which is the subject of dispute possesses a genus that does not subsist in space,
because it has the nature of touch, like a jar. (7 Ātmatva— ) The self is [established] as possessing a genus that does not subsist in space, as is the case with [the aforementioned genus].
[The mind is] the substratum of qualities not perceived by the ear, like a jar. [Mind-ness— ] the subject of dispute— is possessed of a genus that does not reside in the self,
because it is corporeal, like a jar.
(9. The perceptibility of substance-ness, etc.— ) That which is the subject of dispute, namely action, does not exclude the visual perception of the universal [substance-ness],
because it is a sense organ, like the mind.
(10. The nature of color [rūpatva]—) Color-ness is an inherent cause that resides in yellow but does not reside in odor;
for, while being a cause distinct from mere instrumental causes, it is different from odor, like a jar.
(11. The perceptibility of color-ness—)
That which apprehends a genus not graspable by the tactile faculty must be one that has misapprehended [the object],
because it is a sense-faculty distinct from the tactile faculty, just like the mental faculty (manas).
In the same way, the perceptibility of "tasteness" and so forth should also be stated.
(12. Blue-ness—) Blue possesses a genus that does not reside in non-blue forms; for, while having a cause distinct from mere efficient causes, it is distinct from the non-blue, like a jar.
The same should be stated regarding yellowness and so forth.
(13 Taste-ness—) Taste is that which possesses a genus not residing in conjunction;
for, while being a cause distinct from a purely efficient cause, it is other than conjunction, like a jar.
(14 Sweetness—)

The sweet [taste] possesses a genus that does not occur in that which lacks the nature of sweet taste; for, while being a cause distinct from mere efficient causes, it is distinct from non-sweet tastes, like a jar.
This should be stated likewise for bitterness and the other tastes as well.
(15. Odor-ness:
Odor possesses a genus that does not reside in form;
for, while being an exclusive efficient cause, it is distinct from form, like a jar.
(16. Fragrance:
Fragrance possesses a genus that excludes both fragrance and non-fragrance;
for while it is a cause distinct from purely instrumental causes, it is different from non-fragrance, like a jar.
(17. Touchness—) Touch is that which possesses a genus not occurring in taste; for, while being a cause distinct from a purely efficient cause, it is other than taste, like a jar.

(18. Coldness—) Cold is that which possesses a genus not residing in non-cold touch; for, while possessing a cause other than a purely instrumental cause, it is distinct from non-touch, like a jar. The same should be stated regarding non-coldness and so forth.
(19. Number-ness:
Number possesses a genus that does not reside in dimension (*parimāṇa*), because, while having a cause distinct from mere efficient causes, it is different from dimension, like a jar.
The same should be stated regarding duality and so forth.
[Regarding] dimensionality (*parimāṇatva*):
the non-inherent cause, namely magnitude (*mahattva*), possesses a genus that resides in dimension and resides in magnitudes occurring in numbers.
[The argument for separateness: Being a cause distinct from both efficient and inherent causes, while being distinct from number, it is like that [substance].
(21. Separateness—) Separateness is a non-inherent cause; it possesses a genus that resides in a single instance of separateness occurring within dimension, yet is distinct from that [dimension].
Because, while being distinct from dimension (*parimāṇa*), it is a cause that is distinct from a mere efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), just like that [substance];
and this should also be stated regarding singularity (*eka-pṛthaktva*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no presence of a universal (*sāmānya*) in those cases.

Even if the terms "single separateness" (*ekapṛthaktva*) and "double separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) could be accounted for otherwise, it would be impossible to determine that single separateness is the cause for the production of double separateness without another regulating universal (*niyāmaka-aparajāti*);
this is because there is no means of establishing the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
(22. *Saṃyogatva*—)

That which is wrongly understood as a non-inherent cause possesses a genus that does not reside in separateness (*pṛthaktva*), because, while being a cause distinct from purely instrumental causes, it is other than separateness— just like that [separateness].
(23 *Vibhāgatva*--) Disjunction (*vibhāga*) possesses a genus that does not reside in conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

[The subject] is distinct from conjunction because, while being distinct from conjunction, it is the non-inherent cause of a dyad, like a two-threaded cloth. (24 *Paratva*— ) *Paratva* possesses a genus that does not reside in disjunction,
because it is the non-inherent cause of conjunction.

The same should be stated regarding the cognitions of "otherness" (*aparatva*), "nearness" (*paratva*), and so forth; likewise, the previous inference should be stated for gravity (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), viscidity (*sneha*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (25. The perceptibility of Brahminhood)
That which is the subject of dispute is the grasper of a genus that does not reside in varnas other than the Brāhmaṇa,
because it is a sense organ, like the eye.
(26 [Brāhmaṇatva])

A Brāhmaṇa is the substratum of the genus "non-Brāhmaṇa human," because, while being distinct from non-Brāhmaṇa humans, he is a composite whole, like a cow. The disputed continuum of bodies is not born from a womb, [because it is a continuum].
Since it is a bodily continuum,

like the bodily continuum of a scorpion produced from cow dung— by such an inference, if the term "Brāhmaṇa" were found in some cases to be preceded by a non-Brāhmaṇa, then the term "Brāhmaṇa" would not be based on a body produced by a Brāhmaṇa.
In this same way, the refutation of adventitious [causes] should also be stated regarding the status of a Śūdra and so forth.
(27. Action-ness: Throwing upward possesses a genus distinct from the genus of throwing downward and so forth, which is the substratum of qualities;
for, while being a cause other than a purely efficient cause, it is not a quality, like a jar.
[Objection: But if "action" alone is taken as the subject of the proposition, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to air and the like.
Even if those who do not hold a contrary view were included in the class [of subjects], the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would remain unestablished;
rather, there would simply be another, distinct universal (*sāmānya*) inherent in both the object and the wind.
This is not so, for it is not the case that their ultimate homogeneity (*ekajātīyatva*) is what is being proven here.
However, [the object of this cognition] is merely a genus distinct from quality, substratum, and upward motion;
and since it is determined through the exclusion of unity and plurality,
when a distinct genus is entailed by such proofs as "because of possessing a genus residing in space," this [cognition] is accounted for even by taking that [space] as its object.
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for an additional [universal] following after air and so forth.
However, that which is being established by this [reasoning] with respect to action does not exceed the nature of action (*karmatva*);
for its essence consists either in its not residing in qualities while residing in all actions, or in its being distinct from the universal "throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇatva*).

Since such [a property] is perceived here, the term "disputed" (*vipratipanna*) is employed in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in the proof of mere action (*kevalakarmatva*) with respect to air and so forth.
Because it apprehends the distinction residing in air and so forth as presented by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), there is no non-establishment of action-ness;
however, a question may arise regarding air and the like.
Other reasons and further arguments for the theorists (kathaka) should also be investigated;
this same principle should be applied to the case of color-form (rūpa) and so forth as well.

Therefore, since the intended [definition] is established, it is sufficient to say that "color-ness" (rūpatva) is the state of not subsisting in odor while subsisting in yellow, non-yellow, and so on.
Generality (sāmānya) is that which, being eternal, inheres in many [individuals].
[Section on the Category of Particularity (viśeṣa):
That which is the subject of dispute possesses inherence distinct from quality and generality.
Because it is a substance, like a jar.
A particular (*viśeṣa*) is devoid of universals (*niḥsāmānya*) and inheres in a single [substance]. [The definition of inherence (*samavāya*):]
The subject of dispute is connected with a pot,
because it is a substance, like the self;
[and] the subject of dispute is connected by an eternal connection.

Because it possesses substantiality, like space; for the Bhaṭṭas accept an eternal relationship between space and sound, and therefore there is no lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) in that case. There is disagreement only regarding whether the relationship is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), not regarding the substratum (*dharmin*).
Others, however, state that conjunction is distinct from any relation other than itself, because it is an object of cognition (*meyatvāt*).
But what, then, is the supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) here?
[First of all,] there is no impossibility of a cognition of co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), for that does not depend on a relation in general,
nor on the absence of a relation, since such a cognition is absent in the case of a rope and a jar, as well as the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.
If it is argued that this [connection] is based on both difference and non-difference,
then while a difference between the jar and its form is indeed admitted, what, moreover, would constitute their non-difference?
Is it the absence of difference, its contradiction, or something other than that?
It cannot be the first, because of contradiction.

Not the second [alternative], for there would have to be a contradiction based on the substratum, based on the essential nature, or based on the effect; since that contradiction would persist in every respect.
But in the second case, let that [inherence] itself suffice; what is the use of this first [relation]?
As for the third, since it is not distinct from inherence, there is no disagreement regarding it.
If it is argued that the mutual absence between a jar and its form does not exist [therein], [we reply:]...
To say that "there is difference" while "mutual non-existence does not exist" is contradictory, because the two terms are synonymous.
If difference were the very nature [of the thing],
then it would be impossible for the cognition of that [difference] to depend upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
Nor can it be either the first or the second [of the alternatives].
Because it would follow that both the jar and its form would be non-existent; nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, for their effect would then be mere cognition.
Or is it something distinct from that?
In that case, does its existence reside in that very [locus] while being opposed to the other, or does it depend on something distinct from it?
In the first case, there could never be a cognition of both.
Because that contradiction would persist at all times;
as for the second case, let it be just so—what is the use of this [distinction]? But in the third case, the very arising of cognitions is difficult to establish.
Whatever is denoted by a term different from another is distinct with respect to that [other], just as the color residing in a jar is distinct with respect to the jar itself.
The sounds under dispute are inherent in space alone by way of inherence, because they are inherent,
like sound and space.
Nor does the oneness of inherence (samavāya) entail the consequence of a confusion of entities, because it is postulated precisely as that which prevents the confusion of the entire universe;
for its nature was not previously determined, since it is imperceptible.
If it is argued that "the other" exists because one thing possesses a diverse nature, we say no; for such a thing has a single nature, just like a variegated color.
Furthermore, due to the parsimony of conceptual construction (*kalpanālāghava*), the permanence of inherence (*samavāya*) is accepted by the opponent in some cases.
Therefore, its inherence is eternal,
because its oneness has been established.
Inherence is not perceptible to people such as ourselves.
Because it is a relation between that which is perceptible and that which is imperceptible, like the relation between a jar and space;
inherence (samavāya) is an eternal relation.
The state of being an object of the cognition "it exists here.
[Section on the Category of Non-existence:
It is not appropriate for you to say that even that which is known through the cognition "it does not exist" is not accepted by you.
Furthermore, since we also accept the existence of omniscient knowledge (*kevalajñāna*),
that too must be refuted through analysis:
the effect of falling and so forth is produced solely from a cause that generates the absence of an obstructing factor, because it is an effect, just like burning and other such effects.

The linguistic usage "the ground is devoid of a jar" has as its object something distinct from the ground, because it is a usage concerning the ground while being distinct from the mere usage "the ground. This proof is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the usage "the ground [is here]";
nevertheless, non-existence (*abhāva*) must be admitted, since the usage of non-existence is observed even in the absence of a cognition of a "mere" [ground].

For even when a jar and its color are perceived together, there occurs a distinct linguistic usage of their difference, such as "the color is not the jar," and yet in that case there is no cognition of [the jar] alone.
This is because, even when the substratum is not grasped, there is the linguistic usage of the absence of light in all the intervening spaces.
Because even a blind person, through the touch of a hand in the dark, observes the conventional usage of the absence of material form;
furthermore, the eye is a grasper of that which is distinct from the object graspable by the eye,
because it is a sense faculty (*indriya*).
It is fourfold,
distinguished as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Non-existence is differentiated according to the difference in its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
This is because those things that are previously associated with or subsequently associated through identity possess the status of counter-correlates (*pratiyogitva*).
Otherwise, it would be difficult to establish the causality of the absence of an impediment (*pratibandhakābhāva*),
since even absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is included within mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
And since that [non-existence] exists even when there is an obstruction [to its cause], it is non-deviant. Non-inherence is the absence of inherence;
[this constitutes the refutation of non-existence as a distinct category].
(1. Refutation of potency as a distinct category:
If it is argued that potency is also a distinct category of reality, we say no, because there is no means of valid cognition for its existence.
If it is argued that the theory of *sphoṭa* is untenable, we say no;
for it is tenable even in the absence of a [necessary] connection.

And in that regard, the dilemmas concerning prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth are to be resolved by means of the general principle of the non-perception of capacity (*yogyatānupalabdhi*).

Even though the *sphoṭa* arises through the acceptance of the *kāryalakṣaṇā* (indication by effect) of the incantation (*mantra*) which acts as an auxiliary, there is no lack of determinacy regarding its cause.

Furthermore, in the case of the accusative in "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), it does not denote a refinement (*saṃskāra*) inherent in those grains; nor does the fact that [the object] possesses the fruit produced by the action imply that it must be the substratum (*samavāyin*) of that [refinement].
Rather, it implies merely that [the object] is for the sake of that [action].
Otherwise, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by the oblation (*homa*) of the grass-bundle (*prastara*) and other items that have already been employed would not belong to them,
because they have perished.
And yet, it is not the case that there is no state of being the object of refinement (*saṃskāryatva*) in their regard.

According to the principle that "a substance deserves refinement only when it has been or will be put to use," and since it is impossible for a refinement to persist without a substratum, one must postulate that its substratum is the self (*ātman*).
Let it be the same in the other case as well; what is the harm?
(2. Refutation of *jñātatā* as a distinct category:

In the system of the Prābhākaras, regarding the cognition "I know the jar," since there is no effect produced by the cognition residing in the jar, it must be considered how the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established therein.
If it is argued that for this very reason the Bhāṭṭas accept *jñātatā* [as the basis for objecthood], [the response follows].
What then is the status of those [words] that are past or future?
If it is argued that there is no fault because birth (jāti) persists even there,
how then can there be "knownness" (jñātatva) in the individual instance (vyakti)?
If it is argued that this is because there is no difference between the two, we say no,
because a difference also exists.
If it is argued that there is no fault even if there is a difference, we say no.
For it would follow that by the mere cognition of taste through the sense of taste, its substratum would also be cognized;
and by the mere cognition of existence (*sattā*), even one blind from birth would have the cognition of color.
