If it is asked, "Since you do not admit *jñātatā* (the state of being known), how is there a restriction of the object for cognition? [we reply as follows:]
How is there a restriction of the locus for *jñātatā* itself?
If you say it is by the power of its cause, the same solution applies.
(3. Refutation of qualifiedness as a distinct category:
By this, qualifiedness (*viśiṣṭatā*) is also refuted, because the very causal complex that produces [the cognition of] that [qualifier] is sufficient for the arising of a heterogeneous cognition.
Nor is it impossible for there to be a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) in the absence of a difference in object,
because that would entail the consequence that experience (*anubhava*) and memory (*smṛti*) are not of different kinds;
furthermore, if memory had a greater object, it would follow that memory itself is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is impossible for a specific quality that is not [inherently] connected to abide in past or future things, because of the absence of a substratum.
(4. Refutation of the objecthood [of the thing] as a distinct category:)

By this, the relation consisting of the state of being an object (*viṣayībhāva*) is refuted, since the restriction between cognition and its object is established by that very [relation] which governs it. In the same way, proximity (*sānnidhya*) and other such relations are also to be rejected.
(5. Refutation of similarity as a distinct category:
If it is argued that similarity, therefore, must be a distinct category, we say no, because there is a lack of evidence.
Furthermore, conventional usage is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because it is established even through relations such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
How, then, is there the conventional usage of "similarity" with respect to a universal?
Why is there an extension [of ritual details] in the passage, "One should pile the Śyenacit" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.11)?
Because even there, only a similarity of form (*vyakti-sādṛśya*) is perceived.
And because the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word,
the performance of that which possesses two or three properties inherent in the single object "śyena" is possible;
for the apprehension of the convention is justifiable, as in the case of words used with reference to limiting conditions (upādhi).
(6. Refutation of Primordial Matter as a distinct category: In this same manner, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other such entities are also to be rejected, because there is no proof for them.
Nor should it be argued that "the subject of dispute is not produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), either directly or indirectly, because it is an effect"— this is an *avīta* [inference]—
because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.

Nor is it correct to argue that pleasure, pain, and delusion must have a cause because they are effects, for this reasoning is subject to deviation in the case of conjunction and other such phenomena.
Nor is its existence established by an investigation into the production of an existent,
because there is dispute regarding that very point; nor does it possess existence therein simply because it is being employed for that purpose.
Because there is deviation regarding efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*),
and because the operation of a cause is not purposeful when [the effect] already exists, the systematic determination made by one who knows the rules of *jāti* is established.

By the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through which the existence of a jar is established, the absence of a cloth in the threads prior to the production of the cloth is also established by means of "perception of the capable" (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
If there is a suspicion of non-perception due to unfitness [of the object], who could prevent the possibility of it occurring elsewhere as well?
There is no fault of infinite regress in the claim that production arises from the final auxiliary cause in relation to the effect,
because there is no destruction of the root.

Nor is there a contradiction with the charge of tautology, because it is admitted that she (the power) arises from jars and other such things. However, regarding manifestation, since all manifestations would be eternal, there would be the predicament of the impossibility of distinguishing between what is seen and what is unseen. What more need be said? For according to the maxim, "When there is mutual contradiction, no third alternative can exist," other categories of entities could not possibly come into being.
"Because the seven characteristics are mutually contradictory.

In that context, when there is knowledge of the nature of things—such as substances—in terms of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, one perceives the abundance of suffering within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); thus, even pleasure, because it is accompanied by suffering, is categorized under the side of suffering.

And by means of the *upaniṣads*, one who has realized the identity of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and Brahman according to the perspective stated in the *Vaiśeṣika*, whose mind is devoted to the Lord (*bhagavadbhakti*), whose internal obstacles have been destroyed by the glance of a true guru (*sadguru*),

who is eager for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Supreme Lord, who practices meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) day and night, whose knowledge has become fully matured through the course of infinite time, who possesses the dharma born of supreme yoga, who has somehow directly perceived the Supreme Lord, and whose false knowledge has been rendered devoid of opportunity by the growth of its opposite— [for such a person...]

Due to the absence of causes, there is an absence of all suffering for one who has eliminated the possibility of the activity of passion and hatred; thus, there occurs abiding in one's own true nature.
This is what is designated as "liberation" by the wise.
Nor does it follow that there is no engagement [with reality] because of the absence of pleasure.
For even for you, pleasure does not cause [the world] to proceed;
indeed, it cannot be produced by it, because that would contradict its eternity.

For no one exerts effort toward that which is already established; thus, even for you, it is precisely the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) that is to be accomplished through volitional action (*kṛti*).
Consequently, that alone is the *prayojana* (purpose), as it has been said: "That object aiming at which one acts is the *prayojana*" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.24).

The statement, "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is manifested in liberation," is somehow a figurative description (*guṇavāda*)— either with the intention of referring to the happiness born of contentment through a secondary mode of expression (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), or with the intention of referring to the absence of suffering—
because of the scriptural declaration: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.1).
Nor is that [desire] intended for worldly happiness,
because even worldly happiness is not distinct from the bliss of Brahman;
and if it were self-luminous, it would follow that there would be no distinction between one's own liberation and saṃsāra.

On this point, some might say that for the sake of avoiding suffering, the relationship of object and subject between knowledge and pleasure is untenable prior [to liberation] and must be produced subsequently.
That is incorrect,
because there is no evidence for its existence [in that state].
It is also impossible for that which is not well-known in the world to be a motivator;
for there is no such knowledge here.
It has never been observed before that there is a relationship of object and subject [between the self and cognition],
because it is the causal complex of knowledge itself— whether through a statement or otherwise— that produces that [knowledge].
By the very refutation of Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and other such causes, one should understand that the liberation taught by them is also refuted.
The subject of dispute is sometimes devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*),
because it is the substratum of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and because it is the substratum of impermanent specific qualities, like the mind and like space.
Nor is it correct to argue that individual souls (*jīva*) possess eternal knowledge, like the Self (*ātman*) or the Lord (*īśvara*).
This is because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is of the very nature of the Lord (*īśvara*), and there is no deviation from the individual body (*piṇḍa*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not "possessors of eternal specific qualities" (*nityaviśeṣaguṇādhāra*).
The probans "possessing a specific quality" (viśeṣaguṇavattva) is over-narrow because it is limited by the condition of being the originator of a non-terrestrial dyad;
for you, moreover, this [probans] lacks its qualifying attribute, since [pleasure] is devoid of a specific quality.
Thus, "the nature of pleasure" (sukhatva) is inherent in the eternal.
As for the argument "because it belongs to that class," it is inconclusive due to the presence of inferiority within those very things; enough of this over-extension.
Homage to Śambhu, whose matted locks are graced by the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā);
homage to you, the ordainer of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world.
Thus ends the *Mānamanohara*, composed by the venerable teacher Vādivāgīśvara.
